title: Czechia - Blue Street Signs (Plonkit)
description: The street signs in Šumperk can be recognized by being blue, with text filling out almost the entire sign.

title: Czechia - Streets Downtown Prague (Plonkit)
description: Streets in downtown Prague are commonly paved with grey and white marble stones, which is also typical for Portugal. They’re often arranged in intricate square mosaics, but some sections are far more plain.

title: Denmark - License Plate Types (Plonkit)
description: Standard plates are long and white, with a blue strip on the left. Commercial plates are yellow. And so-called “Parrot” plates have a yellow section on the left hand side. These are unique to Denmark.

title: Denmark - General Landscape (Plonkit)
description: Denmark is a generally flat country with wide, open fields between towns. Suburban areas are usually open, with space between buildings. Urban cores are more dense and built up.

title: Denmark - White Road Lines (Plonkit)
description: Denmark has all-white road lines. Double middle lines are very common.

title: Denmark - Square Dashed Outer Lines (Plonkit)
description: Outer road lines often consist of small white squares. These unique-looking lines are a good way to identify Denmark.

title: Denmark - Pipe-Framed Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Denmark has very unique-looking direction signs that are very useful to recognize the country. They are low to the ground and framed by pipes. They are either coloured red and white or blue and white, with a directional arrow incorporated into the background. Signs often feature road numbers.
Some larger road signs have a more standard layout without the pipe frame. Highway signs have blue or green backgrounds.

title: Denmark - Blue Street Signs & '-vej' (Plonkit)
description: Most Danish street names end in “vej.” This is the Danish word for “street.” Street signs most commonly have a blue background with white text.

title: Denmark - Unique Danish Bollards (Plonkit)
description: Denmark has a very recognizable white bollard with a yellow reflector and a dark orange stripe. This bollard is unique to the country. You may also find this green variant.

title: Denmark - Language Features (Plonkit)
description:
Danish is a North Germanic language that is closely related to Swedish and Norwegian. The Danish alphabet contains these special letters: Æ, Ø, and Å.
- Norwegian uses Æ, Ø, and Å.
- Faroese uses Æ and Ø but not Å.
- Icelandic only uses Æ.
- Swedish only uses Å. In addition, Swedish uses Ä and Ö, which are not found in Danish.

title: Denmark - Red Brick Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Much of the architecture in Denmark consists of red brick. Roofs often have orange, dark brown or black tiles.

title: Denmark - Thatched & Corrugated Roofs (Plonkit)
description:
Some houses in Denmark have thatched roofs, especially in rural areas.
You can also sometimes find grey corrugated roofs. These look somewhat similar to roofs commonly found in Baltic countries.

title: Denmark - Timber Frame Buildings (Plonkit)
description: Some older or rural buildings have timber frame walls.

title: Denmark - Pipe-Bent Signposts (Plonkit)
description: This signpost, where the pipe frame is bent around the sign, is unique to Denmark.

title: Denmark - Square Guardrails (Plonkit)
description: Denmark has square (normal B-type) guardrails, with no reflectors.

title: Denmark - 5-Stripe Pedestrian Sign (Plonkit)
description: This Danish pedestrian sign has 5 stripes. Uniquely, the first and fifth stripe touch the edge of the white triangle.

title: Denmark - Town Entry/Exit Sign (Plonkit)
description: This unique sign is found when entering a town. When leaving, there will be a red slash through the sign.

title: Denmark - Bus Stop Signs (Plonkit)
description: Bus stop signs in Denmark are black and yellow. A small sign is attached to the top of the pole, with the bus schedule underneath. Additionally, you may see this older blue and white version.

title: Denmark - Red & White Chevrons (Plonkit)
description: This red-and-white chevron is found in Denmark. They are often low to the ground.

title: Denmark - Lack of Utility Poles (Plonkit)
description: Standard street level utility poles are rare in Denmark. Most of the electricity infrastructure you will find in the countryside are large, towering overhead power lines, often near highways.

title: Denmark - Bicycle Paths (Plonkit)
description: You may sometimes see bicycle paths on the side of the road.

title: Denmark - PostNord Postal Boxes (Plonkit)
description: The PostNord, or Post Danmark company, is the national provider of postal services in Denmark. It uses these unique postal boxes.

title: Denmark - Gas Stations (Plonkit)
description:
These four gas station brands are common to Denmark, but each are shared between one other country:
- Ingo can be found in Denmark and Sweden.
- Ok can be found in Denmark and the Netherlands.
- Uno-X and Yx can be found in Denmark and Norway.

title: Denmark - Stone Bicycle Path Bollards (Plonkit)
description: You will rarely see these stone bollards, which may be painted red at the top, near bicycle paths.

title: Denmark - Road Numbering System (Plonkit)
description:
Denmark has an easy to learn road numbering system. They order their roads from east to west.
Roads starting with the numbers 2 to 5 are grouped by region.
Roads starting with the number 1 can be found nationwide, but the second digit still follows a rough regional distribution. Notably, Bornholm only has roads starting with the number 1.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Denmark - Ring Road Numbering (Plonkit)
description:
Ring roads are special highways near bigger cities, labelled from O1 up to O4. The number increases from the centre, and each fully or partially encircles the city.
These cities have ring roads: Copenhagen, Odense, Aarhus, Aalborg, Hillerød, Kolding, and Velje.

title: Denmark - Regional Bus Companies (Plonkit)
description:
There are six regions in Denmark that each use a different bus transportation company. Each bus will have the brand written on the front, and have a unique colour scheme.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Denmark - Regional Bus Stops (Plonkit)
description:
In addition, these regions each have their own bus stop sign.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Denmark - Greenland Guide (Plonkit)
description:
Greenland is the world’s largest island country, and is a part of Denmark.
A separate Plonk It guide to Greenland can be found here.

title: Denmark - Faroe Islands Guide (Plonkit)
description:
The Faroe Islands is a group of united islands in the North Atlantic, and are an autonomous territory of Denmark.
A separate Plonk It guide to Faroe Islands can be found here.

title: Denmark - Bornholm Bus Stops (Plonkit)
description: The bus stops on the island of Bornholm have this unique green, red and white colour scheme.

title: Denmark - Bornholm Bicycle Signs (Plonkit)
description: These green bicycle signs are found on the island of Bornholm.

title: Denmark - Læsø Seaweed Roofs (Plonkit)
description: These traditional “seaweed roofs” are found on the island of Læsø. They are made from a type of seaweed known as eelgrass.

title: Denmark - Anholt Gen 2 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: The island of Anholt only has Generation 2 coverage, with distinct gloomy, overcast weather. A large portion of coverage is recognizable due to the sandy dirt on the roadside.

title: Denmark - Danish Language Chars (Plonkit)
description: Danish is a North Germanic language that is closely related to Swedish and Norwegian. The Danish alphabet contains these special letters: Æ, Ø, and Å.

title: Estonia - License Plates (Plonkit)
description: Estonian licence plates are long and white, with the standard blue European strip on the left.

title: Estonia - Road Bollards (Plonkit)
description:
Estonian bollards have a round, baton-like shape.
They have a rectangular reflector on the front and two circular reflectors on the back. The reflectors can be white or orange.
!!This infographic shows the main similarities and differences between the bollards of the Baltic and Nordic countries.

title: Estonia - Utility Pole Variety (Plonkit)
description:
Estonia uses a variety of different poles and poletops. Of the three Baltic countries, it has the least consistent utility poles.
Round wooden poles are the most common, sometimes with diagonal supports.

title: Estonia - Square Concrete Poles (Plonkit)
description: You can additionally find a fair amount of square concrete poles, often also with diagonal supports. These are similar to those found in Lithuania.

title: Estonia - Trident Pole Tops (Plonkit)
description: Trident pole tops are somewhat common: This pole top features one insulator on top, and two to the side.

title: Estonia - Pole Top Caps (Plonkit)
description: Most wooden poles have a small metal cap on top, similar to those found in the Nordic countries.

title: Estonia - Road Markings (Plonkit)
description:
Outer road lines sometimes consist of short dashes.
!!In addition, Sweden primarily uses short dashes as outer road lines.

title: Estonia - Red-White Chevrons (Plonkit)
description:
Estonia uses red chevrons with white arrows.
!!However, Latvian and Lithuanian chevrons have the opposite colour scheme: they are white with red arrows.

title: Estonia - Kilometer Marker Angle (Plonkit)
description:
All Baltic countries use the same blue kilometre marker. However, they can be distinguished from each other by their angle relative to the road.
In Estonia, the marker will be perpendicular to the road. It has numbers on both sides of the marker.
For a quick overview of all three Baltic countries, see this infographic.

title: Estonia - Thin Red Sign Border (Plonkit)
description:
Each Baltic country has a slightly different border for its warning and speed signs.
Estonian signs have a thin red border, with no white outline around it (the red border extends all the way to the edge of the sign).

title: Estonia - A-Type Guardrails (Plonkit)
description: Estonia has normal A-type guardrails with no reflectors.

title: Estonia - Estonian Pedestrian Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Estonian pedestrian signs have 3 stripes. The shape of the pedestrian has a relatively high level of detail, detailing shoes and an attached head.
!!Latvian pedestrian signs have 5 stripes.

title: Estonia - Bus Stop Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Estonian bus stop signs have this design.
The bus has four windows. This is mostly useful to distinguish it from the Latvian bus stop sign, which has five windows.
Note, however, that Lithuania has the same bus stop signs as Estonia.

title: Estonia - Blue & White Pole Wrappings (Plonkit)
description: These blue and white signpost wrappings are very common in Estonia.

title: Estonia - Language Characteristics (Plonkit)
description:
Estonian belongs to the Finnic languages, a branch of the Uralic language family. It is closely related to Finnish.
Within the Baltic languages, the following letters are unique to Estonian:
- Vowels with umlauts (two dots): Ä Ö Ü.
- Õ with a tilde.

title: Estonia - Street Naming ('Tänav/Tee') (Plonkit)
description:
The Estonian words for street and road are tänav and tee, respectively. These words are unique to Estonian. Tänav is often abbreviated as ‘tn’.
Many streets, especially in urban areas, have a simple name that completely lacks the tänav and or tee suffix.

title: Estonia - Oval Blue House Numbers (Plonkit)
description: It is fairly common to find oval-shaped blue house numbers in Estonia.

title: Estonia - Wood & White Brick Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Estonian architecture generally consists of a combination of wood and white brick, typically with somewhat steep corrugated metal roofs. Painted stone walls are also somewhat common. While wooden buildings can be found in all three Baltic countries, they are more common in Estonia.

title: Estonia - Directional Signs (Plonkit)
description: Directional signs in Estonia are blue with white text and a white outline.

title: Estonia - Gen 3 Coverage (Plonkit)
description:
Generation 3 coverage in Estonia often has a slight green tint to part of the panorama, which is referred to as “green blur” by the community.
For many players, this green blur can be hard to identify at first. The location shown in this tip’s image is a fairly extreme example. To familiarise you with how it might look in-game, here are some more examples where it is fairly visible: 1, 2, 3, 4.
!!It can however also be found in Sweden, often on the island of Gotland.

title: Estonia - Rural Gen 3 Coverage (Plonkit)
description:
The Generation 3 coverage in Estonia is more extensive than the other two Baltic countries, meaning that a lot of very rural roads are covered. As a result, if you are considering guessing in one of the Baltic countries, and your location is Generation 3 on a very thin and rural road, you are slightly more likely to be in Estonia.
Of course, use caution. This meta has many variables, and is not always reliable. Only use it as a last resort in no-info Baltic roulette rounds, when you have no better clues available.

title: Estonia - Hilly Areas (Plonkit)
description:
Estonia is a fairly flat country throughout, with only 10% of the country being higher than 100 metres, and the highest point being 318 metres tall.
Still, the hilly parts can sometimes be recognizable. The hilliest areas are in the southeast, and the southern half of Lääne-Viru County. Note that the colours of this map are highly exaggerated to show the location of the hills more clearly.

title: Estonia - Russian Cyrillic Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Estonia has a large Russian minority. In most of Ida-Viru County, they form a majority. As a result, you will sometimes see bilingual signs with Russian Cyrillic and Estonian in the region in and around Narva.
Note that the majority of signs will still be in Estonian. You may occasionally see Cyrillic in other places.

title: Estonia - Tallinn Old Town (Plonkit)
description: The old town of Tallinn looks very different from any other urban area in Estonia. It is an almost perfectly preserved historic area, with lots of medieval and renaissance-era buildings. In places, it can look a lot like cities in central Europe.

title: Estonia - Kihnu Fall Coverage (Plonkit)
description:
Kihnu is a small island off the coast that has recognizable coverage:
- All coverage is Generation 4, taken during late autumn (recognizable by the fallen brown leaves on the ground).
- Noticeably, it has a very moody, dark cloud cover, taken close to sunset.
If you see a combination of these two things, Kihnu is a good place to guess.

title: Estonia - Estonian Bollards (Plonkit)
description:
Estonian bollards have a round, baton-like shape.

They have a rectangular reflector on the front and two circular reflectors on the back. The reflectors can be white or orange.

title: Estonia - Short Dashed Outer Lines (Plonkit)
description: Outer road lines sometimes consist of short dashes.

title: Estonia - Chevron Color Scheme (Plonkit)
description: Estonia uses red chevrons with white arrows.

title: Estonia - 3-Stripe Pedestrian Sign (Plonkit)
description: Estonian pedestrian signs have 3 stripes. The shape of the pedestrian has a relatively high level of detail, detailing shoes and an attached head.

title: Estonia - Gen 3 Green Tint (Plonkit)
description:
Generation 3 coverage in Estonia often has a slight green tint to part of the panorama, which is referred to as “green blur” by the community.

For many players, this green blur can be hard to identify at first. The location shown in this tip’s image is a fairly extreme example. To familiarise you with how it might look in-game, here are some more examples where it is fairly visible: 1, 2, 3, 4.

title: Faroe Islands - Mountain Terrain (Plonkit)
description: The landscape of the Faroe islands is characterised by long, wide fjords with jagged green mountains that rise straight out of the water, with rocky ridge lines along the mountainsides. The mountains generally look more imposing and greener than coastal mountains in Iceland, which can often be used to tell them apart.

title: Faroe Islands - Faroe Islands Have (Plonkit)
description: The Faroe islands have almost no naturally growing trees.

title: Faroe Islands - Pickup Truck Meta (Plonkit)
description: The generation 4 coverage was captured with a black pickup truck with an antenna on the front. The truck is always blurred.

title: Faroe Islands - Gen 3 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: All Generation 3 car coverage on the Faroe Islands has a black Street View car with a plain grey roof rack.

title: Faroe Islands - Faroese Houses Typically (Plonkit)
description: Faroese houses are typically made of wood, often with an above ground basement made of stone which is painted in a different colour than the wooden part. Roofs will usually be either metal or have grass on top (turf).

title: Faroe Islands - Language Features (Plonkit)
description: The Faroese language is most closely related to Icelandic, with the special letters Á, Ð, Í, Ó, Ú, Ý, Æ and Ø. It differs from Icelandic by using the letter Ø, while Icelandic uses É and Þ.

title: Faroe Islands - Road Bollards (Plonkit)
description: Faroese bollards are small wooden sticks that are mainly painted yellow and sometimes red on the top.

title: Faroe Islands - Road Guardrails (Plonkit)
description: Guardrails on the Faroes have yellow reflectors.

title: Faroe Islands - Iceland Features (Plonkit)
description: Directional signs are yellow with a thin black border and a metal frame, very similar to the ones in Iceland.

title: Faroe Islands - Torshavn By Far (Plonkit)
description: Torshavn is by far the biggest town on the islands, and the only place where you will find buildings taller than three floors. The landscape is somewhat open relative to the rest of the country, particularly to the east.

title: Faroe Islands - Klaksvik City (Plonkit)
description: Klaksvik is the second biggest town in the country by a significant margin and can often be recognized by the narrow fjord with fairly steep hills going roughly north to south.

title: Faroe Islands - There Three Wind (Plonkit)
description: There are three wind parks visible on the Faroes. The largest one by far is northwest of Torshavn, while the other two are northeast of Torshavn and east of Vestmanna respectively.

title: Faroe Islands - Village Kirkjubøur (Plonkit)
description: The village of Kirkjubøur at the southern tip of the main island can be recognised by the black houses, almost all having grass roofs. The town also has a small church ruin.

title: Faroe Islands - Trekker Koltur Island (Plonkit)
description: The trekker on Koltur island can typically be recognized by the narrow and low peninsula on the southeastern tip of the island.

title: Faroe Islands - Trekker Eiðiskollur Be (Plonkit)
description: The trekker on Eiðiskollur can be recognized by the extremely low clouds surrounding the peninsula.

title: Faroe Islands - Trekker West Skopun (Plonkit)
description: The trekker west of Skopun can be recognised by the wide strait to the north with the main islands of the Faroes in the background.

title: Faroe Islands - Snow-Capped Mountains (Plonkit)
description: There are two distinct pyramid-shaped mountains to the south of the trekker on Klakkur, with a very thin layer of snow on top.

title: Faroe Islands - Snow-Capped Mountains (Plonkit)
description: The trekker by Gjógv features a view of the village to the south with snow covered mountains in the background.

title: Faroe Islands - Grey Boat Featuring (Plonkit)
description: A grey boat featuring several people in reflective clothes and with the text “RIB62” can be seen going to Koltur island.

title: Faroe Islands - Iceland Features (Plonkit)
description: Directional signs are yellow with a thin white border, identical to the ones in Iceland.

title: Finland - License Plate Dimensions (Plonkit)
description: Finland has shorter than normal white plates with the standard European blue strip on the left.

title: Finland - Solid White Outer Lines (Plonkit)
description: Where present, outer road lines will always be solid white lines.

title: Finland - Yellow Middle Lines (Plonkit)
description:
Finland has several different types of middle road lines, including:
- white dashes, with or without a solid white line next to it
- solid yellow with white dashes
- double yellow.
Yellow lines are being phased out and are increasingly rare in newer coverage.

title: Finland - Black & White Bollards (Plonkit)
description: Finland has long black-and-white bollards with a rectangular, white reflector on the front and two dots on the back. They can be either round or thin and curved. The black strip is typically diagonal.

title: Finland - Orange Snow Poles (Plonkit)
description: In Finland, it is common to find orange snow poles with a thin white band near the top.

title: Finland - Finnish Language Chars (Plonkit)
description: The Finnish language is not related to most other European languages, so it has a very unique look. It has a lot of long words and double vowels. The Finnish alphabet includes the letters ä and ö.

title: Finland - Street Names ('-tie/katu') (Plonkit)
description: Most Finnish street names end in “tie” or “katu.” These are the Finnish words for road and street. Street signs most commonly have a white background with black text.

title: Finland - Yellow Sign Backgrounds (Plonkit)
description: Finnish road signs have a yellow background.

title: Finland - Yellow Stroke on Signs (Plonkit)
description: On traffic signs that have a red border, you will find a thin yellow stroke on the edge of the sign.

title: Finland - 5-Stripe Pedestrian Sign (Plonkit)
description: Finnish pedestrian signs have 5 stripes.

title: Finland - Blue Directional Signs (Plonkit)
description: Finnish directional signs consist of a solid blue background, white text, and a white border with guiding arrows.

title: Finland - Black & Yellow Chevrons (Plonkit)
description: Finnish chevrons are black with yellow arrows.

title: Finland - Wooden Utility Poles (Plonkit)
description: Finland primarily uses wooden utility poles. Most of them tend to have a simple design, but they can have a variety of poletops. Poles often have a street light attached to them.

title: Finland - Double-Bolted Lamps (Plonkit)
description: Lamps attached to wooden poles in Finland are normally mounted to the top of the pole with a double bolting.

title: Finland - Blue/White Signpost Stripes (Plonkit)
description: Traffic signposts often have blue and white striped markings.

title: Finland - Birch & Pine Forests (Plonkit)
description: Most of Finland is covered by dense boreal forests. Pine trees are common, as well as birches, which are easily recognizable by their white trunks.

title: Finland - Gen 2 Coverage (Plonkit)
description:
A lot of Generation 3 coverage was taken in autumn, meaning that trees in this coverage often have distinct fall colours.
Take note that this season meta is not present in Generation 2 and Generation 4 coverage.

title: Finland - Abundance of Lakes (Plonkit)
description: Lakes are so common in Finland, that the country is also sometimes known as the Land of a Thousand Lakes. Usually, you do not have to drive long to find a body of water.

title: Finland - Modern & Wooden Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Finnish architecture is mostly modern and utilitarian. Downtown areas tend to be very modern, with lots of apartment buildings and use of concrete. Suburbs mostly consist of freestanding single family homes. Many houses have wooden cladding. Like Sweden and Norway, some wooden buildings, especially in the countryside, are painted in a distinctive dark red colour.

title: Finland - Bus Stop Signs (Plonkit)
description: Finland has two styles of bus stop signs, a blue and white one, and a yellow and black one.

title: Finland - Supermarket Chains (Plonkit)
description:
K-Market and S-Market are two Finnish supermarket chains with recognizable logos. Both chains operate only in Finland.
K-Market is sometimes known as K-Supermarket or K-Citymarket.

title: Finland - Shitcam (Low Quality) (Plonkit)
description: Google used a weird, low-quality camera in Finland. This camera is known as the official Ari (or “Shitcam”). It has a wide circular car blur, and can be distinguished from Generation 2 by its lack of a sky halo and often somewhat brownish colours. A good map will not usually include this coverage, but it is good to be aware of its existence, in order to not be caught off-guard by it.

title: Finland - Smallcam Coverage (Plonkit)
description: Finland also has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.

title: Finland - Regional Road Numbering (Plonkit)
description:
Finnish regional roads have 3- or 4-digit road numbers. The first digit of those road numbers is region-specific. These regions are distributed in a rough south-to-north order, starting from 1 in the south to 9 in the north.
These road numbers often appear on direction signs. Learning the regions can help with cutting down on scanning time for 5k’s, or give you a rough region to plonk in during quick no move games.

title: Finland - Lapland Snow Poles (Plonkit)
description: Snow poles which have 2 long reflectors can be found on bigger roads in Lapland.

title: Finland - Coastal Farmlands (Plonkit)
description: Finland has a lot of farmlands, but the majority of them are concentrated near the west and south coast.

title: Finland - West Coast Wind Turbines (Plonkit)
description: Wind turbines are most commonly found along the west coast of Finland, with some exceptions.

title: Finland - Northern Stunted Trees (Plonkit)
description: Small, stunted trees with spindly, thin trunks are common in northern Finland.

title: Finland - Lapland Gen 3 Snow (Plonkit)
description: Generation 3 snow coverage is only found in far northwestern Lapland.

title: Finland - Swedish Speaking Areas (Plonkit)
description: The Swedish language is common in some coastal areas in the south and the west. In these areas, bilingual Swedish or Finnish texts are common. If you see Swedish language in a Finnish setting, do not guess inland.

title: Finland - Sámi Languages (Plonkit)
description: The Sámi languages are spoken in the far north of Finland. In this region, you can sometimes find bilingual signs with place names in both Finnish and Sámi. Unlike Finnish, its alphabet uses the letter c.

title: Finland - Southwest Tilted Antenna (Plonkit)
description: This slightly tilted, long antenna can be found in southwestern Finland.

title: Finland - South-Central No Antenna (Plonkit)
description: Generation 3 coverage with no antenna at all can be found in south-central Finland.

title: Finland - Åland Islands Status (Plonkit)
description: Åland is a group of islands off the southwestern coast. It is an autonomous, mostly self-governing region of Finland with its own flag. Though it has a special status, for country streaks purposes it is still counted as part of Finland.

title: Finland - Åland Swedish Language (Plonkit)
description: Åland is monolingually Swedish. If you see only Swedish, and no Finnish language, but you suspect that you are in Finland, consider the Åland Islands.

title: Finland - Åland Road Features (Plonkit)
description: Åland roads have two unique aspects that separate them from the rest of Finland: their pavement tends to have a red tint, and they have dashed outside road lines that resemble those found in Sweden.

title: Finland - Åland License Plates (Plonkit)
description: Licence plates on Åland are white with blue text, making them appear almost completely white on Street View. They are noticeably quite short and lack the European blue strip on the left side.

title: Finland - Åland Pedestrian Signs (Plonkit)
description: Some pedestrian signs on Åland have four stripes, with the exact same design found in Sweden. Beware that many pedestrian signs will still be the typical Finnish design.

title: Finland - Åland Bus Stops (Plonkit)
description: Bus stops on Åland include a white plate with 4 numbers. Some also include this semicircle sign on top.

title: Finland - Road 970 (North) (Plonkit)
description: Road 970 in the far north, on the border with Norway, is easily recognizable: it runs through a river valley with hills on both sides. The river is visible in many places, usually to the northwest. The birch trees around the road are small and stunted.

title: Finland - Kilpisjärvi Landscape (Plonkit)
description: Due to its proximity to the Scandinavian Mountains, the area near Kilpisjärvi features a unique hilly landscape, with low vegetation.

title: Finland - Helsinki Sidewalk Trekker (Plonkit)
description: Downtown Helsinki has a lot of Generation 4 sidewalk trekker coverage.

title: Finland - Helsinki Trams (Plonkit)
description: Helsinki features these unique green-and-yellow trams.

title: Finland - Helsinki Buses (Plonkit)
description: The buses in and around Helsinki are typically blue-and-white, with a vertical split. Buses elsewhere can have the same colour scheme, so look for one of these logos on the bus.

title: Finland - Tampere Buses (Plonkit)
description: The buses in and around Tampere are blue on the bottom and white on the top. The word ‘NYSSE’ is written on the sides of the buses.

title: Finland - Turku Buses (Plonkit)
description: Buses in Turku are uniquely yellow, with a white rear.

title: Finland - Jyväskylä Buses (Plonkit)
description: Buses in Jyväskylä are almost completely green.

title: Finland - Oulu Buses (Plonkit)
description: Buses in Oulu have a pink front.

title: Finland - Street Lamps (Plonkit)
description: You can find Red rectangular metallic plates with 7 golden or dark red coloured protrusions that form a rounded hexagon shape on houses, lamp posts, and signposts in Tampere.

title: Finland - Seinäjoki Street Signs (Plonkit)
description: This style of blue street sign with white text is unique to the cities of Seinäjoki and Isokyrö southeast of Vaasa.

title: Finland - Lahti Street Signs (Plonkit)
description: Lahti uses these street signs with a black border and all capital letters.

title: Finland - Kerava Coat of Arms (Plonkit)
description: The city of Kerava uses street signs with this blue-and-yellow coat of arms in the top-left corner.

title: Finland - Järvenpää Coat of Arms (Plonkit)
description: The city of Järvenpää uses street signs with this blue-and-grey coat of arms in the top-left corner. The neighbourhood name is also written above the street name.

title: Finland - Fall Colors (Gen 3) (Plonkit)
description: A lot of Generation 3 coverage was taken in autumn, meaning that trees in this coverage often have distinct fall colours.

title: Finland - Tampere Metallic Plates (Plonkit)
description: You can find these unique metallic plates on houses, lamp posts, and signposts in Tampere.

title: France - License Plate Stripes (Plonkit)
description:
Modern French plates are long and white, with blue strips on both sides of the plate. The left strip will be more visible than the right strip.
Some older French plates lack the right blue strip, with the rear plate being yellow. These are very rare in newer coverage.

title: France - French Language Chars (Plonkit)
description:
French is a Romance language that is closely related to languages like Catalan, Spanish and Italian. It uses these diacritics and special letters:
- Accent aigu: é
- Accent grave: à, è, ù
- Accent circonflexe: â, ê, î, ô, û
- Trema: ë, ï, ü, ÿ
- Ligature: œ
- Cédille: ç with a small hook
In addition, the -ux suffix is only found in French.

title: France - Street Name ('Rue') (Plonkit)
description: The French word for street is “rue”.

title: France - White Bollard w/ Red Band (Plonkit)
description: The French bollard is extremely recognizable and appears very often. It is a round white post with a pointed top and a reflector band going all the way around. The band can be grey or red. Some rare variations have a fully red top.

title: France - Double-Indented Bollard (Plonkit)
description:
A different round white bollard, with two reflective indented bands, is unique to France.
You can also find this design in other colours like green or yellow.

title: France - Wedge-Shaped Bollard (Plonkit)
description: Less common wedge-shaped bollards with wide rectangular white reflectors on both the front and back are also unique to France.

title: France - Ladder Poles (Plonkit)
description: Concrete poles with step-like indents are common in France. They are referred to as ladder or waffle poles by the community.

title: France - Rural Wooden Poles (Plonkit)
description: Wooden poles and thin octagonal metal poles are very common in rural areas and small towns.

title: France - Blue Pole Stickers (Plonkit)
description:
Small blue rectangular markings on utility poles are unique to France. They are often referred to as ‘stickers’ by the community, but are actually small plates.
You will find these plates on almost all wooden and metallic poles, but not as often on ladder poles.

title: France - French Poletops (Plonkit)
description: Diamond shaped pole tops with three wires are commonly called “French poletops” within the community. They are most frequently found on top of ladder poles.

title: France - Arrowhead Insulators (Plonkit)
description: Some variations of the French pole tops have the insulators on top. These variations may resemble an arrowhead and are unique to France.

title: France - Smallcam Coverage (Plonkit)
description: France has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.

title: France - Yellow D-Road Signs (Plonkit)
description: Small yellow signs displaying the road number, which typically starts with a “D”, are unique to France. They are commonly placed on top of directional signs or town entry signs.

title: France - Directional Signs (Plonkit)
description:
French directional signs are usually white with a black outline slightly offset from the edge. They have an arrow-like shape, with the black border getting thicker at the point.
Highway directions have either a blue or green background.
Smaller places and points of interest are frequently written in an italic font.

title: France - Town Entrance Signs (Plonkit)
description: Town entrance signs in France have a red border with a thin white outline.

title: France - Red Border Signs (Plonkit)
description: French road signs have a red border with a thin white outline. You will often find white rectangular signs with black text below traffic signs.

title: France - Flat Signposts (Plonkit)
description:
Many traffic signs in France have flat rectangular signposts.
Signposts, along with signbacks, can be dyed with unorthodox colours, more so than in other countries. Some of those are regional, which you can learn more about in the regionguessing section.

title: France - Short Signposts (Plonkit)
description: Traffic signs with particularly short signposts are very common in France.

title: France - Multi-Arrow Chevrons (Plonkit)
description: France uses chevrons with white arrows on a blue background. They can have a wide amount of arrows, ranging from one to five.

title: France - 5-Stripe Pedestrian Sign (Plonkit)
description:
Pedestrian crossing signs in France have five stripes and a disconnected head on the person. They have the usual white border of French traffic signs.
Less commonly, you can find a design with two dashed lines instead of stripes.

title: France - Kilometer Markers (Plonkit)
description: Kilometre markers in France most commonly have a yellow or red semicircle on top of a white rectangle. They can be found in the form of a waystone or as a flat sign and can be either parallel or perpendicular to the road. Major highways can have square markers with a red top.

title: France - Outer Road Dashes (Plonkit)
description: Typical French roads have long spaced out dashes on the outside.

title: France - Offset Block Lines (Plonkit)
description: These middle road lines, where each dash consists of two offset blocks, are unique to France. They are not extremely common, but when you see them, you can safely guess France.

title: France - Long Dashed Lines (Plonkit)
description: Middle lines with dashes that are longer than usual can be a good clue for France.

title: France - Passing Zone Arrows (Plonkit)
description: These arrows on the road signalling the end of a passing zone are only found in a couple of European countries, including France. In France, the middle dashes will be very close together in these areas.

title: France - A-Type Guardrails (Plonkit)
description: France uses A-type guardrails, usually without reflectors. On rare occasions, you can find thin B-type, the standard guardrail in Czechia and Slovakia.

title: France - Austrian Flag Markers (Plonkit)
description: Roads may be lined by tall rectangles on a stick in the colours of the Austrian flag, which are not found elsewhere.

title: France - Stone & Pastel Houses (Plonkit)
description:
French architecture largely consists of stone houses, which will normally be either unpainted or painted in greyish or yellow pastel colours. The roofs will typically have a simple gable design, with orange tiles or less commonly black slates. Townhouses will often lay wall to wall along the road.
Do note that France has some of the most diverse regional architecture of any European country, so don’t be surprised to see towns that look significantly different from the previously described architecture.

title: France - Blue House Numbers (Plonkit)
description: House numbers in France are most commonly blue, typically written in a serif font with slightly exaggerated shapes. This is most useful when differentiating from Italy, which almost never uses blue house number signs.

title: France - Domestic Car Brands (Plonkit)
description: French car brands Peugeot, Renault and Citroën together make up almost half of all cars in France.

title: France - Administrative Divisions (Plonkit)
description:
This guide will mainly operate with two types of administrative divisions: regions, totalling at 13 in European France, and 96 departments, which appear on google maps as the primary administrative divisions. Other rarer divisions you may come across include pre 2016 regions, historical provinces, and regions based on cardinal directions.
Departments are often named after physical geographical features and their logos may show up on various infrastructure, shown in the next tip.
You can practise them with this quiz.

title: France - Phone Area Codes (Plonkit)
description:
French telephone numbers are 10 digits long, with the first two pairs of digits being two separate area codes, following two patterns:
- 01 is in Île-de-France and 02-05 goes clockwise from the northwest.
- 2X is in the far north, with the numbers generally increasing anticlockwise. 9X is an exception, being found both in the far northwest and far southeast.
Secondary area codes in Île-de-France can be seen on this map.

title: France - Department Numbers (Plonkit)
description: Each department has an assigned number to it, arranged mostly alphabetically. This is most useful in postal codes, consisting of 5 digits, the first two representing the department they’re in.

title: France - Department Logos (Plonkit)
description:
Most departments have their own unique logo (formally called official flag), often containing stylized initials or the entire name. Notable infrastructure with department logos include bus stops, kilometre markers, trail banners, directional signs and signbacks. Learning what each logo looks like is not recommended for beginners, but it can be helpful to know what they stand for when scanning.
You can find the full list of logos here, or see them projected onto a map here.

title: France - Occitanie Flag (Plonkit)
description:
A red and yellow logo with an Occitan cross and vertical stripes is the official flag of the Occitanie region.
The rest of the regions also have logos, which appear less frequently. You can see them projected onto a map here.

title: France - Pyrénées-Orientales Flag (Plonkit)
description: A flag made up of red and yellow stripes, based on the Senyera, is the official flag and department logo of Pyrénées-Orientales. You will often find the pattern used in coats of arms on street signs.

title: France - Red Tinted Roads (Plonkit)
description: Roads with a significant red, purple or burgundy tint are most commonly found in an area between Paris and Dijon, with Normandy being a notable exception. The historical region of Burgundy, which gave the name to the shade of red, roughly corresponds to the highlighted area.

title: France - Green Signposts (Plonkit)
description: Dark green road signposts and backs are most commonly found in Brittany and around Paris, but also various southern regions in the country.

title: France - Green Sticker Signbacks (Plonkit)
description: Signbacks in Eure-et-Loir may include a green sticker, the department’s logo. They’re usually placed on a dark green back, without a matching post.

title: France - Decimal D-Roads (Plonkit)
description: Still in Eure-et-Loir, this is also where D-roads with a superscript number are most common. On the map, these are expressed as decimals, e.g. D134.10 and D121.9.

title: France - Grey-Green Signbacks (Plonkit)
description: A greyish green signback supported by a darker green post, is found in three areas: Brittany (Côtes-d'Armor and eastern half of Ille-et-Vilaine), Pyrénées-Atlantiques and rarely near the Alps.

title: France - Pas-de-Calais Signs (Plonkit)
description: In the Pas-de-Calais department, you may find road signs with the following colour arrangement: a dark green post paired with a signback of a lighter shade of green, ranging from matcha green to greenish turquoise. The department’s logo, a green and blue triangle, is occasionally present on the signback.

title: France - Brown Signposts (Plonkit)
description: Road signs where both the post and back are painted brown are most commonly found in Seine-et-Marne, and rarely in Ille-et-Vilaine. It is more reliable when the post is square, however round signposts are equally common.

title: France - Burgundy Attachments (Plonkit)
description: Directional signs in Haute-Garonne often use burgundy red attachments and ornaments. This is sometimes paired with yellow signposts.

title: France - Combined Entry Signs (Plonkit)
description: Most town entry signs in Marne follow a unique format: Instead of having separate entry and exit signs, they are combined into a single, noticeably thicker block.

title: France - Paris Suburb Signs (Plonkit)
description: Street signs in the metropolitan area of Paris often say the name of the city, which is generally atypical for street signs in France. The signs will often be made in a modern design, and many city names will be river based, notably named after Seine and Marne.

title: France - Corsican Stone Barriers (Plonkit)
description: Cuboid barriers made of stones and mortar are commonly found on Corsica. While by no means unique to Corsica, it is good to consider the island when you see them in rounds with a plausible Mediterranean landscape.

title: France - Topography Map (Plonkit)
description: This is a topographic map of France. Notably, the tallest mountains are found in the southeast and on the Spanish border. The north and the west coast is generally quite flat or rolling, while the southern half is often hillier.

title: France - Normandy Hedges (Plonkit)
description: Rural roads surrounded by hedges blocking the view, reminiscent of the British Isles, are primarily found in the northwest, particularly in Normandy.

title: France - Southern Stone Pines (Plonkit)
description: Stone pines are commonly found along the southern coast, often planted alongside urban roads. You may however find them as north as Nantes.

title: France - Landes Pine Forests (Plonkit)
description: Forests made up entirely of Maritime pines (pinus pinaster) are found in the southwest of the country (Gironde and Landes departments). The whole area will be fairly flat, which is not typical of other areas with such pines.

title: France - Wine Regions (Plonkit)
description: France is the second largest wine producer in the world, with many famed wine regions. The most common include the area around Bordeaux, southern coast and Champagne, East of Paris. Other regions include, but are not limited to, Loire Valley, Alsace and Corsica.

title: France - Southwest Sunflowers (Plonkit)
description: Sunflowers are mostly found in the southwest of the country, particularly around Toulouse.

title: France - Northern Wind Turbines (Plonkit)
description: Wind turbines are considerably more common in the north of the country.

title: France - Northwest Black Roofs (Plonkit)
description: Black shingle roofs are primarily found in the northwest, the rough cutoff being the Loire river. Other areas include near the Belgian border, the south-centre, and the Pyrenees, making black roofs a good clue for Alps-Pyrenees toss-ups.

title: France - Brittany Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Brittany has one of the most recognizable and consistent architectures in the country. Common elements include, in addition to black roofs, edge chimneys, black slate walls and stones surrounding doors and windows. The walls will be either very light coloured or made of stone.

title: France - Southern Tiled Roofs (Plonkit)
description: Roofs in the south of the country will often be made up of rounded tiles overlapping one another, often varying in colour.

title: France - Red Brick Rows (Plonkit)
description: Rows of dark red brick houses, most similar to Flemish architecture in Belgium, are unsurprisingly found near the Belgian border. The individual bricks may be outlined by white mortar.

title: France - Toulouse Orange Bricks (Plonkit)
description: In and around Toulouse, mainly in old towns, you will commonly find bright orange brick buildings. They differ from brick houses near Belgium by the bricks being brighter, as well as somewhat Mediterranean looking architectural features, such as wooden shutters, being common.

title: France - Paris Area Stone Walls (Plonkit)
description: Walls made of uneven cream coloured to orange stones, glued with mortar and often incorporating red brick details can be found in the towns surrounding Paris. Note that the city of Paris itself generally does not have this architecture.

title: France - French Riviera Architecture (Plonkit)
description: The French Riviera will mirror many characteristics of Monaco. Rich areas with planted palms and light coloured multi story buildings with wide balconies are good indications you’re in this area, with the rest of the southern coast and Corsican Bastia sharing similar vibes.

title: France - Basque Timber Framing (Plonkit)
description: White houses with, often colourful, timber framing are a staple of Basque architecture that extends beyond the Basque speaking area. The timber frame colour (in this case red) will be consistent with other wooden elements, like window shutters and gates.

title: France - Alpine Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Alpine architecture, unmistakable for its light coloured base and extensive wooden elements, is unsurprisingly found in the Alps.

title: France - Alsatian Architecture (Plonkit)
description:
Many elements of Germanic architecture are concentrated in Alsace, such as timber framing and half-hip roof. Furthermore, roofs with fish scale tiles are more common in this region.
Beware that these elements are sometimes incorporated into architecture in other parts of France, and are most reliable in conjunction with one another.

title: France - Regional Languages (Plonkit)
description:
France is home to many minority languages, 6 of which will be covered in this guide:
- Alsatian, a dialect of Alemannic German.
- Basque, the only European language isolate.
- Breton, a Celtic language.
- Catalan, Corsican and Occitan, Romance languages which are related to French.
However, French, legally the only official language, is dominant in all regions of the country, so don’t exclude highlighted regions when you’re placed in an all French round.

title: France - Breton Language Signs (Plonkit)
description: Breton is a Celtic language, visually most similar to Welsh. Common letters include d, k, w and the letter ñ, which is not found in French. It is commonly found on the Breton peninsula, with bilingual street signs as east as Rennes and rarely Nantes. The Breton word for street is straed.

title: France - Plou- Towns Prefix (Plonkit)
description: Towns with the Plou- prefix are concentrated in Northwestern Brittany.

title: France - Alsatian Language Signs (Plonkit)
description: Alsatian, a dialect of German, is occasionally found in Alsace, a region that changed countries 4 times in modern history. Most bilingual street signs use some variation of gasse or strasse.

title: France - Occitan Language Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Occitan is a Romance language closely related to Catalan that’s sparsely concentrated in the South of France, most often found on street signs in big cities, and very rarely on town entry signs. It can be divided into dialects, each using a slightly different word for street, all similar to Catalan “carrer”. For example, in Toulouse, you’ll find the Languedocian carrièra and in Avignon carriero, in the Provençal dialect.
Click here for a more extensive infographic.

title: France - Basque Language Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Bilingual signs in Basque, a language isolate, are concentrated In the western half of the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department, bordering the Basque speaking regions in Spain. Common letters include K, X and Z. On directional signs, it’s written with a thinner font, which is unique within all minority languages in France.
The word for street is karrika, in contrast to “kalea” in the Spanish Basque country.

title: France - Corsican Language (Plonkit)
description: On the island of Corsica, you may find bilingual signs in Corsican, a Romance language that utilises many features found in Italian, like words almost always ending in vowels. In particular, the endings u/iu/ju, changed from o/io, are common in Corsican. Moreover, placenames will usually have an Italian origin.

title: France - Catalan Language (Plonkit)
description:
The far southern department Pyrénées-Orientales, also known as Catalunya Nord (Northern Catalonia), uses Catalan on their various signage.
It is closely related to both Spanish and French, with Ç being considerably more common than in French. The word for street is carrer.

title: France - Toponymy Suffixes (Plonkit)
description:
Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. This map shows one of the most common and useful endings, with rare exceptions. Other, extraordinarily rare suffixes can be found here.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: France - River/Coastal Toponyms (Plonkit)
description:
Many French cities contain the name of the river they lay on, usually in the format -sur-[river]. On signage, sur are often shortened to ˢ/, in this case Chalonnes-sur-Loire (Chalonnes upon Loire). The picture shows five of the longest and therefore most common origins of river based names, but cities can bear the name of any river, regardless of length.
Similarly, city names containing -sur-mer (=on sea) or -plage (=beach) are found exclusively on the coast.

title: France - Réunion Overview (Plonkit)
description:
Réunion is an overseas department and region of France, east of Madagascar. As such, it is counted as France for country streaks purposes.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Réunion here.

title: France - Saint-Pierre & Miquelon (Plonkit)
description:
Saint-Pierre and Miquelon is a self-governing territorial overseas collectivity of France, south of Newfoundland in Canada. As such, for country streaks purposes, it is counted as France.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Saint-Pierre and Miquelon here.

title: France - Martinique Overview (Plonkit)
description:
Martinique is an overseas department and region and a single territorial collectivity of France, in the eastern Caribbean. For country streaks purposes, it is counted as France.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Martinique here.

title: France - Parisian Mansard Roofs (Plonkit)
description: Mansard roofs, also known as French windows, are a very common feature of Parisian architecture. They’re made up of steep black shingle roofs with inserted dormer windows. While not unique to Paris, it is a good clue in abundance and on wide boulevards.

title: France - Belle-Île-en-Mer (Plonkit)
description: On the Breton island Belle-Île-en-Mer you can find houses typical for Brittany combined with colourful façades and outlines, superficially similar to houses in Portugal.

title: France - Lavender Fields (Plonkit)
description: Lavender fields can be found in the southeast, appearing as small grey bushes when not fully grown.

title: France - Atlantic Salt Farms (Plonkit)
description: Salt farms, which appear as flooded trenches with grass medians, are found along the Atlantic coast, most notably around Guérande, Noirmoutier, Île de Ré and Île d'Oléron.

title: France - Arrondissement Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Paris, Lyon and Marseille are the three largest cities in France and the only ones divided into municipal arrondissements (Arrᵗ or Arrt. for short). The arrondissements appear on google maps, so finding these street signs can help a lot with pinpointing.
The street signs of these three cities will be further described in the following tips.

title: France - Paris Street Signs (Plonkit)
description: Paris uses an iconic green & Prussian blue design with a top arch that has also been replicated in Bucharest, which is sometimes referred to as Paris of the east.

title: France - Lyon Street Signs (Plonkit)
description: Lyon’s street signs feature four corner bolts and an uninterrupted inner white border that cuts a notch for the arrondissement and each bolt.

title: France - Marseille Street Signs (Plonkit)
description: Marseille’s street signs will usually feature the city’s emblem, a variation of the Greek cross. The white border will usually be interrupted at the top, even when the cross is absent.

title: France - Bordeaux Arrondissements (Plonkit)
description: Small tables with “Arrᵗ” written on a small separate sign, are found in Bordeaux, despite being a city not divided into arrondissements.

title: France - Montpellier Street Signs (Plonkit)
description: Montpellier street signs will typically contain a blue ‘M’ on a white background in the top left corner.

title: France - Lille Street Signs (Plonkit)
description: Street signs with a red slanted fleur-de-lis are unique to Lille.

title: France - Bordeaux Red Posts (Plonkit)
description: In the outskirts of Bordeaux, you may find square traffic signposts with the Bordeaux shade of red, named after the wine grown in the region.

title: France - Riviera Blue Posts (Plonkit)
description: On the French Riviera (Côte d'Azur in French, literally translated as Blue Coast), you can find regular traffic signposts painted azure blue. Uniquely, Cagnes-sur-mer, west of Nice, will feature lighter, powder blue infrastructure.

title: France - Northern Thin B-Guardrails (Plonkit)
description: Thin B type guardrail, typical for Czechia and Slovakia, is sometimes found on highways in the northern half of the country, often coming from Le Mans, Tours, Paris, Reims and Metz.

title: France - Gen 3 Antenna Flags (Plonkit)
description: On rare occasions, you may find a flag attached to the antenna in the generation 3 coverage. While much of the highlighted areas has been overwritten, learning the distribution of each antenna can yield very high scores.

title: Germany - Gen 4 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: All car coverage in Germany was taken with a Generation 4 camera.

title: Germany - Black & White Bollards (Plonkit)
description: Germany uses these black and white bollards, with white and light-grey reflectors. The reflector will be orange on bollards next to intersections. They sometimes have plates containing the road number, and potentially other useful information. Many bollards also feature blue attachments on the side.

title: Germany - German Language Chars (Plonkit)
description: The official language of Germany is German. The German language uses the special letters Ä, Ö, Ü and ß.

title: Germany - White Pole Sticker (Plonkit)
description: Most wooden poles in Germany will feature a rectangular white sticker.

title: Germany - Common Pole Tops (Plonkit)
description: Germany has a wide variety of different poles and pole tops. The most common pole tops being the horizontal bar with uneven hanging insulators, Triangle pole top, and all kinds of T-shaped pole tops, which can have varying insulator setups.

title: Germany - Dark Grey Sign Backs (Plonkit)
description: Germany also has a wide variety of sign backs. Notably, you can commonly find black or dark grey sign backs, which are rather rare in Europe. Most signs will also feature this sticker, with an upside-down red triangle on a black rectangle.

title: Germany - Bus Stop Signs (H) (Plonkit)
description: Like Austria, Germany uses a wide variety of regional bus stops, all of which have the big yellow and green H symbol on them.

title: Germany - Yellow Mailboxes (Plonkit)
description: Mailboxes in Germany are bright yellow, and feature this black logo.

title: Germany - Bollard Frequency (Plonkit)
description: You will find an excessive amount of bollards on most roads in Germany. Around every 50 metres to be exact.

title: Germany - German Town Entry (Plonkit)
description:
German town entry signs are yellow with black text and have a metallic frame.
- !!The town and/or city name on the top.
- !!The Municipality in the middle.
- !!And the county on the bottom.

title: Germany - Germany Uses Blue (Plonkit)
description: Germany uses these blue rectangular kilometre markers with a white border for A-Roads (Autobahn). B-Roads and local roads have white markers with a black border.

title: Germany - 5-Stripe Pedestrian Sign (Plonkit)
description: German pedestrian signs have five stripes and the person has a belt.

title: Germany - Einbahnstraße Sign (Plonkit)
description: These one-way traffic signs, with the word ‘Einbahnstraße’ written on them, are unique to Germany.

title: Germany - No Stopping Arrows (Plonkit)
description: “No Stopping” and “No Waiting” signs in Germany will often have white arrows drawn on them.

title: Germany - Circular Stickers Usually (Plonkit)
description: Circular stickers, that are usually green, are found on the bottom right of the windshield on almost every car in Germany. Not as useful to know, but they will have the number 4 written on them. They can rarely be yellow or red instead, and will have the numbers 3 and 2 respectively.

title: Germany - Wind Turbine Density (Plonkit)
description: Wind turbines are far more common throughout Germany than in any other European country.

title: Germany - Mountain Terrain (Plonkit)
description:
Using the surrounding elevation can be crucial for getting good guesses in Germany. Here are some general rules:
- The north and especially northwest is very flat.
- Central Germany is hilly.
- Very southern Germany has big mountains.
Also note that despite having a higher elevation, many parts of southern Germany can still be flat.

title: Germany - Phone Area Codes (Plonkit)
description: German area codes are grouped by their first digit. You can practise them by playing this map.

title: Germany - Postal Code Clockwise (Plonkit)
description: Postal codes are arranged in a counter-clockwise fashion, starting with 0 around Saxony and ending with 9 in northern Bavaria and parts of Thuringia.

title: Germany - State Flags (Plonkit)
description: Each German state has their own flag. Many of them are rare to find, though.

title: Germany - State Coats of Arms (Plonkit)
description: Each German state also has their own coat of arms. They are found on unblurred licence plates and some official buildings.

title: Germany - Slavic Place Names (-ow/-itz) (Plonkit)
description: These are some of the more useful and common suffixes for regionguessing Germany. Due to their Slavic origins, endings like -ow and -itz are primarily found in the east, whereas place names ending in -weiler and -ach are mainly located in the southern half.

title: Germany - Guardrail Distribution (A/B) (Plonkit)
description: While most of Germany uses B-Type guardrails, A-type guardrails are common in the northwest, as well as in Rhineland-Palatinate and parts of Bavaria.

title: Germany - Bicycle Sign Colors (Plonkit)
description: Bicycle direction signs typically feature a white background with green lettering. In Hamburg, North Rhine-Westphalia and a neighbouring part of Lower Saxony, you will instead find red lettering. The Saarland has its own distinctive design, with white text on a dark green background.

title: Germany - Folded Sign Backs (Plonkit)
description:
You can use the backs of street signs to regionguess Germany.
Here are examples of a folded, and flat sign back.

title: Germany - Sign Back Connectors (Plonkit)
description: You can also use the sign back connectors on street signs to regionguess Germany.

title: Germany - German Alps (Plonkit)
description: The German Alps is the most mountainous region in Germany, it is mostly concentrated on the Austrian Border.

title: Germany - Northeast Pine Forests (Plonkit)
description: Baltic Pines or Pinus sylvestris are generally more concentrated in the northeast of Germany. They can be recognized by their orange-tinged trunk.

title: Germany - White Bottom Trees (Plonkit)
description: You can spot trees that are painted white close to the bottom of the trunk in the northeast.

title: Germany - Regensburg Ridges (Plonkit)
description: The flat plains southeast of Regensburg can be recognised by the slight ridge often visible to the northeast. The plains themselves are flat, and quite agricultural.

title: Germany - Vineyard Regions (Plonkit)
description: Vineyards are mostly concentrated in the southwest of Germany. However, there are a couple regions further east as well.

title: Germany - Hop Fields (Munich) (Plonkit)
description: You can find hop fields in these regions. They are commonly seen just north of Munich.

title: Germany - Northwest Brick Houses (Plonkit)
description: These brick houses are generally concentrated in northwestern Germany.

title: Germany - Thatched Roofs & Rock Walls (Plonkit)
description: Thatched roofs and rock walls are most common on the North Frisian Islands, as well as mainland Schleswig-Holstein. You can also commonly find them in coastal resort towns in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

title: Germany - Black Slate Walls (Plonkit)
description: Houses with black slate walls, resembling fish scales, are commonly found in a large area of central Germany.

title: Germany - Plattenbau (Commie Blocks) (Plonkit)
description: These large, utilitarian apartment buildings constructed during the socialist era, that are also known as “Commie blocks” are common in all of former East Germany.

title: Germany - Dark Reflector Bollards (Plonkit)
description: Bollards with darker reflectors than usual are found in these regions.

title: Germany - Green Cap Bollards (Plonkit)
description: Some bollards in North Rhine-Westphalia have a green bit at the top. The top can also be another colour.

title: Germany - LVR Green Caps (Plonkit)
description: Some of the green caps will have the text ‘LVR’, along with a small coat of arms. These specific green caps are unique to southern North Rhine-Westphalia.

title: Germany - Bavarian Wooden Bollards (Plonkit)
description: These round wooden bollards, which have a painted top, are found in Bavaria.

title: Germany - Lower Saxony K-Road Bollards (Plonkit)
description: These irregular looking bollards, which do not have a white encasing on the bottom half, are found on K-roads in this region of Lower Saxony. K-Roads in this region will not have any other type of bollard.

title: Germany - Orange Snow Poles (Plonkit)
description: These simple orange posts are most commonly found in Bavaria, and also in the other highlighted states.

title: Germany - Tree Markers (Green) (Plonkit)
description: Many trees in Brandenburg and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern have these tiny green markers on them. You can very rarely find them in Lower Saxony.

title: Germany - Bavarian Road Markers (Plonkit)
description: Bavaria uses these white rectangular road markers, which are divided by black lines into three sections. The left section provides the road you are currently on.

title: Germany - Lower Saxony Markers (Plonkit)
description: You can find these simple rectangular markers, with rounded edges in Lower Saxony.

title: Germany - Metallic Border Markers (Plonkit)
description: These markers with a metallic border around the marker itself are found in Schleswig-Holstein and Lower Saxony.

title: Germany - Triangular Post Variants (Plonkit)
description:
These triangular posts are commonly found in these regions.
You can go more in-depth with them, too.
- Rhineland-Palatinate and Saxony use unpainted, rocky-looking posts, with white plates stuck on each side.
- Saarland, Thuringia, and Baden-Württemberg use white posts, with the same white plates attached. The posts are usually quite tall, except in Baden-Württemberg, where shorter ones are used.
- Baden-Württemberg also uses grey posts.
- North Rhine-Westphalia uses white posts without white plates on the sides. You can also find posts which go all the way to the ground.
- Hesse barely uses these posts at all. However, when they do, it is quite unpredictable.

title: Germany - White Bollard Plates (Plonkit)
description: These basic white plates on bollards can be found in these states.

title: Germany - Black Disk Bollards (Plonkit)
description: Bollards standing on these black disks are commonly found in all of eastern Germany.

title: Germany - Orange Bollard Plates (Plonkit)
description: Rhineland-Palatinate is the only state where the plates on the bollards are orange instead of white.

title: Germany - Grey Bollard Plates (Baden) (Plonkit)
description: Similarly, Baden-Württemberg is the only state where the plates on the bollards can be grey instead of white.

title: Germany - Red Cap Posts (Plonkit)
description: These white posts with a red cap are found in all of former East Germany, but most commonly in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.

title: Germany - Yellow Posts (Brandenburg) (Plonkit)
description: Fully yellow posts are found in the state of Brandenburg.

title: Germany - Yellow Posts with Plates (Plonkit)
description: Yellow posts with a white plate on them are found in Saxony-Anhalt.

title: Germany - Concrete Poles (Plonkit)
description: These round concrete poles are almost unique to former East Germany.

title: Germany - Trident Pole Tops (Plonkit)
description: These trident-like pole tops can be found in Bavaria, Saxony-Anhalt, and Baden-Württemberg.

title: Germany - Triangle Pole Tops (West) (Plonkit)
description: Triangle pole tops similar to the ones in Czechia and Slovakia are common in Western Germany.

title: Germany - Thick Middle Bar Poles (Plonkit)
description: These pole tops where the middle of the horizontal bar is thicker can be found in all of former East Germany.

title: Germany - Curved Bar Poles (Bavaria) (Plonkit)
description: Pole tops which have a curved horizontal bar can be found in Bavaria, though they are rare.

title: Germany - White & Black Gen 4 Car (Plonkit)
description: You can find this rare white and black Generation 4 car in Hamburg and around Frankfurt.

title: Germany - Aldi Equator (Plonkit)
description: There are two regional Aldi chains, which have split Germany in two; Aldi Süd in the south, and Aldi Nord in the north.

title: Germany - City Street Signs (Plonkit)
description:
- Berlin uses white signs with a grey border, and a separate section for numbers under the street name. Also note how the letter ß looks.
- Munich has blue street signs with a white decorative border that does not touch the corners. Also note the unique font.
- Stuttgart uses black signs without a border.
- Düsseldorf has black signs with a white border, similar to Munich. The signs have a metallic frame.
- Dortmund uses blue signs with a white border and a grey frame. The signs also have a separate section for numbers under the street name.
- Essen has blue signs with a very thick metallic frame.
- Dresden has blue signs with a unique font.
- Hanover uses white signs with a wider than usual gap between the sign and metallic frame.
- Nuremberg has blue signs with a unique font. The signs also have a grey frame with a small gap between it and the sign.
- Wuppertal uses white signs with a unique font and a white painted frame with a small gap between it and the sign.
- Mainz has a mix of blue signs, and this unique red variant.
- Frankfurt uses blue street signs with a metallic border around the sign, as well as the separate section for numbers under the street name.

title: Germany - Sorbian Language Signs (Plonkit)
description: Sorbian, a Slavic language, is spoken near the Polish and Czech border. You can find it on a variety of signs in these regions.

title: Germany - City State Bus Stops (Plonkit)
description:
Every city state uses a unique and recognisable bus stop.
- Berlin uses segmented bus stops, with a yellow signpost.
- Hamburg bus stops have a red signpost, and the route numbers are within hexagons. Note that they can be found outside of Hamburg as well.
- Bremen proper uses simple bus stops, which have the bus stop name within a red section. The edges can be rounded.
- Bremerhaven, which is still part of Bremen, uses bus stops with a grey section on the opposite side of the signpost. And the bus stop name is red within a yellow section.

title: Germany - City State Bins (Plonkit)
description:
Every city state has recognisable rubbish bins all around the city.
- Berlin uses bright orange bins that have white text on them.
- Hamburg uses bright red bins, with white speech bubbles.
- Bremen has green and grey bins, with orange speech bubbles.
Bremerhaven uses a more generic green design, with a black logo.

title: Germany - Cologne Lamp Stickers (Plonkit)
description: Lampposts in Cologne will often feature these bright yellow numbers on a black piece of plastic.

title: Germany - Arched Half-Timbered Houses (Plonkit)
description: This type of half-timbered house with arches at the ground floor is very common in this region of Saxony.

title: Germany - Sylt Landscape (Plonkit)
description: The shrub and sand covered hills are unique to the island of Sylt. And like the rest of the North Frisian Islands, rock walls, brick houses, and thatched roofs are common.

title: Germany - Singen Lowcam (Plonkit)
description: Lowcam coverage can be found around Singen and near Switzerland.

title: Germany - Safari Park Gen 3 (Plonkit)
description:
You can find a Generation 3 black car in this safari park southeast of Bielefeld.
You can commonly see 4x4s painted with a zebra pattern in the park.

title: Germany - Hamburg Gen 3 Antenna (Plonkit)
description: This rare Generation 3 car coverage with an antenna can be found in central Hamburg.

title: Germany - Yellow Town Entry Signs (Plonkit)
description: German town entry signs are yellow with black text and have a metallic frame.

title: Germany - Blue Distance Markers (Plonkit)
description: Germany uses these blue rectangular kilometre markers with slightly rounded edges and a white border.

title: Germany - Terrain & Elevation (Plonkit)
description:
Using the surrounding elevation can be crucial to getting good guesses in Germany. Here are some general rules:

The north and especially northwest is very flat.

Central Germany is hilly.

Very southern Germany has big mountains.

Also note that despite having a higher elevation, many parts of southern Germany can still be flat.

title: Germany - East German Concrete Poles (Plonkit)
description: These round concrete poles are almost unique to Former Eastern Germany.

title: Gibraltar - Overview (Plonkit)
description: Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory located at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, bordering Spain. For country streak purposes, the territory is counted as the United Kingdom.

title: Gibraltar - Gibraltar Antenna (Plonkit)
description: All coverage in Gibraltar is Generation 3. The car will always have a unique long antenna with a silver tip, often referred to simply as the “Gibraltar antenna” by the community.

title: Gibraltar - Rock of Gibraltar (Plonkit)
description: The territory’s most recognizable feature is the Rock of Gibraltar, a massive limestone mountain that dominates every part of the territory. It can be recognized by its exposed white limestone rocks and distinct shape.

title: Gibraltar - Like Uk Gibraltar (Plonkit)
description: Like the UK, Gibraltar uses white front and yellow back plates on vehicles.

title: Gibraltar - Driving Side (Right) (Plonkit)
description: Unlike the UK, Gibraltar drives on the right.

title: Gibraltar - English Language (Plonkit)
description: The main language used in Gibraltar is English. This can be especially helpful if you see English on official signs in a Mediterranean setting.

title: Gibraltar - Architecture & Shutters (Plonkit)
description: The urban parts of Gibraltar are mostly fairly dense. Buildings look similar to those found in other Mediterranean countries. They have pastel colours and louvered window shutters (horizontal slats of wood set into a frame). These window shutters are usually painted green, blue or brown.

title: Gibraltar - Christmas Decorations (Plonkit)
description: All coverage is from December, so in many parts of town you will see Christmas decorations.

title: Gibraltar - Barbary Macaques (Plonkit)
description: Gibraltar is famous for its monkeys, of the species Barbary macaque. It is the only place in Europe where you can find wild monkeys.

title: Gibraltar - Ibrahim-al-Ibrahim Mosque (Plonkit)
description: Near the southern tip of the territory, you will be able to see the minarets of the Ibrahim-al-Ibrahim Mosque, the southernmost mosque in continental Europe.

title: Gibraltar - Yellow Rear Plates (Plonkit)
description:
Like the UK, Gibraltar uses yellow back plates on vehicles.

However, note that unlike the UK, Gibraltar drives on the right.

title: Greece - License Plates (Plonkit)
description: Greek licence plates are either all white or have the standard European design, with a blue strip on the left side. Taxis have yellow licence plates.

title: Greece - Dual Script Alphabet (Plonkit)
description: The Greek language features a unique alphabet not used in any other language. It shares similarities with both the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets, however the lower case letters generally have softer shapes than the Cyrillic letters.

title: Greece - Dark Wooden Poles (Plonkit)
description: Greek utility poles are primarily wooden, and often have a distinctly dark brown colour. They will often be noticeably taller than in other countries.

title: Greece - Harp Pole Tops (Plonkit)
description: These distinctive poletops, which have a metal frame shaped vaguely like a harp.

title: Greece - 5-Insulator Poles (Plonkit)
description: Many poles in Greece will have five vertical insulators. They can either be attached to the pole or the metal frames from the previous tip.

title: Greece - Pole-Mounted Lamps (Plonkit)
description: This type of small lamp, attached to the side of poles with a round shade above the light bulb.

title: Greece - Double White Middle Lines (Plonkit)
description: In Greece you will commonly see slightly faded, solid white double middle lines. This can be used to distinguish it from most other Mediterranean countries.

title: Greece - Yellow Edge Lines (Plonkit)
description: Yellow road lines are more common in Greece than any other southern European country.

title: Greece - Wedge-Shaped Bollards (Plonkit)
description: Greek bollards are wedge-shaped with almost square reflectors, being red on the front and white on the back.

title: Greece - Black & White Chevrons (Plonkit)
description: Greek chevrons have white arrows on a black background.

title: Greece - Yellow Warning Signs (Plonkit)
description: Greek warning signs have a red border and a yellow background.

title: Greece - Blue Directional Signs (Plonkit)
description: Greek directional signs are typically blue and arrow shaped. One of the most recognisable features are the place names, which are written in Greek with a yellow font, and in English with a white font.

title: Greece - Town Entry Signs (Plonkit)
description: Greek town entry signs are white with thick horizontal blue stripes at the top and bottom.

title: Greece - Language Features (Plonkit)
description: Greek kilometre markers are blue, having “km” written on the left in both the Latin and Greek alphabets.

title: Greece - Dotted Line Pedestrian Sign (Plonkit)
description: Pedestrian signs have two dotted horizontal lines, rather than vertical stripes.

title: Greece - Roadside Mini-Churches (Plonkit)
description: These types of miniature churches, put on small pedestals, are often found along Greek roads and are unique to Greece.

title: Greece - White Stone Architecture (Plonkit)
description:
Greek architecture shares a lot of features with other Mediterranean countries: a lot of white and pastel-coloured stone houses with orange tiled roofs. White houses are very common when compared to most other Mediterranean countries.
Urban residential buildings will generally be multi-floored, light-coloured and typically have connected balconies along one or multiple walls.
Perhaps the most recognisable style of Greek architecture are the white houses with blue fences, window frames and doors. Beware that these are mainly found on islands.

title: Greece - Mountain Roads (Plonkit)
description: Greece is a very mountainous country, with a large portion of the coverage being taken on winding mountain roads.

title: Greece - Red Soil (Plonkit)
description: Red dirt is very common in Greece.

title: Greece - Smallcam Coverage (Plonkit)
description: Greece has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.

title: Greece - Winter Gen 3 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: Greece has a lot of Generation 3 winter and fall coverage, which tends to look somewhat bleak and depressing.

title: Greece - Island Coverage Map (Plonkit)
description:
Greece is a country with many small islands, some with coverage and some without. Furthermore, while mainland Greece and Crete have all three camera generations, this will not be true for most islands.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Greece - Phone Area Codes (Plonkit)
