description: Greek area codes will always begin with a 2, followed by 1-3 digits determining the area.

title: Greece - Mountain Terrain (Plonkit)
description: The largest flat agricultural valleys in Greece are found close to Thessaloniki and Larissa, but smaller flat valleys, where the mountains generally appear closer, can be found in several other areas in the north and centre of the country.

title: Greece - Western Mountains (Plonkit)
description: The tallest Greek mountains are found in the western half of the country, and contain most of the country’s high-altitude mountain roads with coverage.

title: Greece - Cycladic Architecture (Plonkit)
description: One of the most well-known types of Greek architecture; houses with completely white walls, blue doors and shutters, is mainly found on the small central Cyclade islands.

title: Greece - Barren Central Islands (Plonkit)
description: On many of the central islands you can find a very barren landscape, with small bushes and no trees in sight. This tends to be more common on the smaller islands with coverage.

title: Greece - Olive Plantations (Plonkit)
description: Olive plantations are found in coastal areas, particularly on Crete and southern Peloponnese.

title: Greece - Citrus Plantations (Plonkit)
description: Citrus plantations are mainly found in coastal areas, particularly on southern Peloponnese.

title: Greece - Crete Antenna (Plonkit)
description: On Crete, you may find this unique car antenna, with a slight bulge at the tip.

title: Greece - Mount Pangaion (Plonkit)
description: Mount Pangaion can be recognised from its shape, being more of a solitary mountain rather than a wide mountain range, combined with the fact that it is located to the south of a flat agricultural valley.

title: Greece - Meteora Monoliths (Plonkit)
description: These extraordinary monolithic mountains are called Meteora, and can be found north of Trikala.

title: Greece - Athens Taxis (Yellow) (Plonkit)
description: Yellow taxis are found in Athens.

title: Greece - Thessaloniki Taxis (Blue/White) (Plonkit)
description: Blue taxis with a white roof are found in Thessaloniki.

title: Greece - Thessaloniki Antennas (Plonkit)
description: In Thessaloniki, you will often see a large amount of unusually tall antennas on top of buildings.

title: Greece - Greek Alphabet (Plonkit)
description: The Greek language features a unique alphabet not used in any other language. It shares similarities with both the Latin and Cyrillic alphabet, however the lower case letters generally have softer shapes than the Cyrillic letters.

title: Greece - Blue KM Markers (Plonkit)
description: Greek kilometre markers are blue, having “km” written on the left with both the latin and greek alphabet.

title: Hungary - License Plates (Plonkit)
description:
Hungary uses long white standard European licence plates. Taxi licence plates are yellow.
In July of 2022, Hungary switched to this new character format, which contains the coat of arms.

title: Hungary - Bollards & Reflectors (Plonkit)
description: Hungarian bollards are black-and-white, wedge-shaped, and typically have a red reflector at the front, and a white reflector at the back. Blue reflectors are also somewhat common.

title: Hungary - Holey Concrete Poles (Plonkit)
description: The most common type of utility pole in Hungary is a concrete holey pole, with relatively thin holes going all the way down to the ground. Wooden poles are also somewhat common.

title: Hungary - Chevron Color Scheme (Plonkit)
description:
Hungarian chevrons are white on red.
Black-and-white chevrons may also be seen, but are considerably less common.

title: Hungary - Language Characteristics (Plonkit)
description: The Hungarian language has a unique look, with a very large number of acute accents, umlauts) over o’s, and long words. The letters "Ő" and "Ű", with double acute accents, are unique to the language.

title: Hungary - Street Naming ('Utca/Út') (Plonkit)
description: Hungarian street names typically end with the word “utca”. The word “út” is also used for bigger roads. These two words are unique to Hungarian, and translate to “street.”

title: Hungary - Green KM Markers (Plonkit)
description:
These green kilometre markers can be seen along most Hungarian roads.
On highways, the numbers correspond to the ones seen on the map in small yellow boxes near exits.

title: Hungary - Tall Sign Posts (Plonkit)
description: Hungarian sign posts commonly appear to be abnormally tall, often taller than the Street View camera.

title: Hungary - Sign Bolt Pattern (Plonkit)
description: Hungarian signs are usually bolted to the sign post using four bolts, going through the sign, in the shape of a tall rectangle.

title: Hungary - 5-Stripe Pedestrian Sign (Plonkit)
description:
Hungarian pedestrian crossing signs have five stripes. The person is wearing a belt. There is also a second, less common, type with four stripes and the person holding a bag.
The belt is located noticeably low on the person’s body, almost as if the person is sagging his pants. This is unique to Hungary.

title: Hungary - Road Number Shields (Plonkit)
description: Apart from European highways, there are two types of numbered roads in Hungary; roads marked with green signs, and highways beginning with the letter ‘M’, marked with blue signs. These road numbers are contained within a small shield shape on the sign.

title: Hungary - Directional Signs (Plonkit)
description: Most directional signs are green, having a white inner border and a green outer border. Directional signs on M-numbered highways are blue, having a white inner border and a blue outer border.

title: Hungary - Gen 3 Antenna Flag (Plonkit)
description: It is somewhat common to see a small, grey flag on the antenna of Generation 3 Google cars in Hungary.

title: Hungary - White Gen 4 Car (Plonkit)
description: A white generation 4 Google car can also rarely be found in Hungary.

title: Hungary - Black Gen 4 Car (Plonkit)
description: A black generation 4 car that will never have an antenna can be found in Hungary.

title: Hungary - Winter Gen 3 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: The majority of Generation 3 coverage in Hungary was taken during winter, resulting in very grey, dead looking coverage.

title: Hungary - Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Hungarian houses are typically made of stone, painted in a light colour and almost always with red tiled roofs. Suburban houses are typically only one storeyed, while more central houses may be taller. Houses in town and city centres are often fairly old but well-kept.

title: Hungary - Bike Lane Lines (Plonkit)
description: While Hungarian road lines are all-white, lines on bicycle lanes are typically yellow.

title: Hungary - Phone Area Codes (Plonkit)
description: Hungarian phone numbers consist of either 8 or 10 digits. If the number has 8 digits, the first and second digit is the area code. And if the number has 10 digits, the third and fourth digit is the area code. The only exception is Budapest, where only the first or third digit, being a 1, respectively is the area code.

title: Hungary - Road Numbering System (Plonkit)
description: The first digit of Hungarian numbered roads are ordered in a circle, centred around Budapest. Remembering this system should make it quite easy to find any numbered road.

title: Hungary - Town Name Prefixes (Plonkit)
description:
Many Hungarian town names use local prefixes, the most common of which are shown in this infographic. Note that some rare exceptions exist.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Hungary - Western Metal Frames (Plonkit)
description: If you see a street sign with a thick metal frame around it, you are very likely to be in the western parts of the country.

title: Hungary - Eastern Arrow Signs (Plonkit)
description: If you see a blue or green street sign shaped like an arrow, attached to a utility pole or street light, you are likely to be in the county of Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg.

title: Hungary - Northern Mountains (Plonkit)
description: While the southeastern parts of Hungary are extremely flat, with almost no noticeable hills, the northern and western parts mainly consist of forested hills and mountains. The tallest mountains are found in the north, while the southwestern mountains are generally slightly lower.

title: Hungary - Lake Balaton (Plonkit)
description: Lake Balaton is one of the largest lakes on mainland Europe, and the only large lake visible on street view in Hungary. The area surrounding the lake is moderately hilly, fairly built up and a big tourist destination, with a much higher density of small hotels than almost anywhere else in the country.

title: Hungary - Hortobágy National Park (Plonkit)
description: Unlike most of the Hungarian plains, which is almost entirely cultivated land, the Puszta, centred around Hortobágy National Park, mainly consists of barren and wet, natural grasslands.

title: Hungary - City Street Signs (Plonkit)
description:
This infographic showcases ten of the largest towns and cities with unique street signs, and explains what makes them unique.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Hungary - Slovak Border Road (Plonkit)
description: The road east of Tornanadaska, right by the border to Slovakia, can be easily recognized by the snow on and along the road, combined with the bollards and the railway right next to the road.

title: Iceland - Gen 4 Pickup Truck (Plonkit)
description: The Generation 4 coverage was captured with red and white pickup trucks, which have been well blurred.

title: Iceland - Gen 3 Antenna (Plonkit)
description: The Generation 3 Google car in Iceland is a white car with a long antenna.

title: Iceland - License Plates (Plonkit)
description:
Icelandic licence plates are fully white with blue characters. Unlike most of Europe, the plates do not feature a blue strip on the left.
It can be hard to see the blue of the characters through the blur of the plates.

title: Iceland - Yellow Bollards (Plonkit)
description: Iceland has unique yellow bollards with a white reflector. These bollards are extremely common and can be found throughout the country on almost every section of rural road.

title: Iceland - Volcanic Soil (Plonkit)
description: Iceland often looks barren and treeless. Most regions have a dark grey soil consisting mostly of volcanic rocks.

title: Iceland - Geological Landscape (Plonkit)
description: Iceland is a very geologically active country, where plate tectonics and volcanic processes have shaped the landscape. As a result, many regions are rugged, mountainous and a sight to behold. In addition, strange and bewildering landscapes can be found all over, such as geothermal lakes, lava fields, rift valleys, and towering rock formations.

title: Iceland - Yellow Direction Signs (Plonkit)
description: The road direction signs of Iceland are yellow. They usually have a white inset box that shows the road numbers. If the inset box has a dashed border, the number listed refers to a nearby road, not the road you are currently on.

title: Iceland - Yellow Pedestrian Signs (Plonkit)
description: Icelandic pedestrian signs feature four stripes and often have a slight yellow tint.

title: Iceland - Language Characters (Plonkit)
description: The Icelandic language contains a couple of unique letters. These are some of the most recognizable ones: ð þ and æ. Vowels can have the following accents: á é í ó ö ú ý. The uppercase version of ð is Ð.

title: Iceland - Street Signs (Plonkit)
description: Iceland’s street signs use a white background and black text. They often have a thin metal rim and are attached to lampposts or traffic lights.

title: Iceland - White Road Lines (Plonkit)
description: Iceland has all-white road lines. Outside lines, if present, can be either solid or, more rarely, dashed lines.

title: Iceland - Chevron Color Scheme (Plonkit)
description: Icelandic chevrons are black with yellow arrows.

title: Iceland - Yellow Sign Backgrounds (Plonkit)
description: Just like Sweden and Finland, Icelandic signs feature a yellow background.

title: Iceland - Coverage Map (Plonkit)
description:
Iceland is rather sparsely covered. The southwest region has the densest coverage. Only a few interior roads are covered.
You can click on the image to enlarge it. Alternatively, you can look at the coverage in more detail on this site.

title: Iceland - Road Numbering System (Plonkit)
description:
Iceland has a very sensible road numbering system that allows for quick 5k’s, provided you find the yellow direction signs that list the road numbers of the intersection you are on.
The main ring road, which circles the entire island, simply has the number 1. There are no other roads that start with 1.
The first digit of the other road numbers is region-specific. These regions have a sequential distribution around the island, starting from 2 in the south and increasing up until 9 in a clockwise direction (see map for approximate distribution).

title: Iceland - Westfjords Landscape (Plonkit)
description: The Westfjords region features numerous narrow fjords, surrounded by moderately tall, and mostly flat-topped mountains.

title: Iceland - Eastfjords Landscape (Plonkit)
description: The far east of the country is also home to several fjords. What distinguishes them from the Westfjords are the generally larger and more jagged mountains.

title: Iceland - North Valleys (Plonkit)
description: The mountains west of Akureyri contain many valleys, sandwiched between tall, often slightly snowcapped peaks. Most of these valleys generally face north to northeast.

title: Iceland - Interior Barrenness (Plonkit)
description: Barren landscapes consisting mostly of dark volcanic gravel, with little to no vegetation or signs of life, are typical of the inland regions of Iceland. Most such covered roads are located in the east.

title: Iceland - Southwest Agriculture (Plonkit)
description: The Southwest agricultural area in Iceland can be identified by its relatively flat farmland landscape scattered with numerous farmsteads, fields, meadows and grasslands.

title: Iceland - Hilly Terrain (Plonkit)
description: The wide valley around Eiðar is slightly hilly and agricultural, with tall, snowy peaks visible in the distance on either side, to the east and northwest, respectively.

title: Iceland - Mountain Terrain (Plonkit)
description: The valley around Hallormsstaður has a distinct northeast/southwest angle with low-lying mountains on either side, a wide river flowing through it, and an unusual amount of trees for Iceland. Some of the sideroads are in the forests.

title: Iceland - Mountain Terrain (Plonkit)
description: You can recognise the area near the town of Selfoss from its distinct flat-ridge mountain. Due to the otherwise flat landscape, this mountain can be seen from a wide area.

title: Iceland - Capital City Features (Plonkit)
description: Reykjavík is the capital and by far the largest city in Iceland. The city is mostly flat with slight hills, and is located on the south side of a bay. It is most recognizable as it is significantly larger than other Icelandic cities, with a large urban area and “bigger city” feel.

title: Iceland - Mountain Terrain (Plonkit)
description: Akureyri is the second-biggest city in Iceland and is located in a North-South oriented valley, along the western edge of the bay. The city features mountains ranges to the east and west, making it recognisable.

title: Iceland - White Pickup Meta (Plonkit)
description: Iceland can be split in half depending on the colour of the pickup truck, with red being found in the southwest, and white being found in the northeast.

title: Iceland - Coastal Coverage (Plonkit)
description: The southern coast of Iceland features some impressive glaciers visible from the ring road, spilling into the sea from the Vatnajökull ice cap.

title: Iceland - There Only Handful (Plonkit)
description:
There are only a handful of highways in Iceland which are either divided or have more than two lanes. The divided highways are shown in dark red, while the highways with three or more lanes are shown in bright red.
- Divided roads can be found inside cities other than Reykjavík.
Roads may temporarily be divided close to intersections.

title: Iceland - Coastal Coverage (Plonkit)
description: The Island of Heimaey can easily be recognised by seeing these ragged rocky cliffs overlooking the town of Vestmannaeyjabær. Similar cliffs can be seen on the islands off the coast.

title: Iceland - Very Foggy Coverage (Plonkit)
description: Very foggy coverage can be found around the town of Bakkagerði, in northeastern Iceland. The fog can also be seen from a distance.

title: Iceland - There Only Handful (Plonkit)
description: There are only a handful of highways in Iceland which are either divided or have more than two lanes. The divided highways are shown in dark red, while the highways with three or more lanes are shown in bright red.

title: Ireland - License Plates (Plonkit)
description:
Ireland has long, white licence plates with the standard European blue strip on the left.
The white backplate is especially useful to distinguish it from the UK, which uses yellow backplates (but white fronts). In addition, most UK vehicles lack the blue strip on the left.

title: Ireland - Yellow Dashed Edge Lines (Plonkit)
description: It is very common to see yellow outside dashes on Irish roads.

title: Ireland - Architecture (Plonkit)
description: You will usually find cream white buildings with black roofs in Ireland. Sometimes, the buildings feature grey corner stones. In cities, you will typically find row buildings.

title: Ireland - Yellow Diamond Warnings (Plonkit)
description:
Ireland is the only European country that uses yellow diamond-shaped warning signs.
Note that this only applies to warning signs. Regulatory signs (circles and upside down triangles) have the normal red border and white background, like most other European countries.

title: Ireland - Bilingual Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Irish signage is often bilingual, with English in a regular font, and Irish in italics. Place names, regular words and phrases are all translated.
Irish language is somewhat less common on non-official signage.

title: Ireland - Chevron Color Scheme (Plonkit)
description: Irish chevrons are yellow on black. Both single and multiple arrows are common.

title: Ireland - Yellow Warning Stickers (Plonkit)
description:
The yellow warning stickers on utility poles can be a good way to distinguish between Ireland and the UK.
The most important difference is that UK stickers feature a guy getting zapped by a lightning bolt.
The Irish stickers usually have a lightning bolt, but lack the guy getting zapped. They also often have an extra second rectangular sticker with a black outline, below the lightning bolt.

title: Ireland - Yield Sign Text (Plonkit)
description: Irish yield signs feature the word “YIELD”.

title: Ireland - Green & White Bollards (Plonkit)
description: These green and white bollards can be a good clue for Ireland. They are not entirely unique to the country, but they are especially helpful in 50-50s with the UK.

title: Ireland - Rounded Metal Gates (Plonkit)
description: Rural metal gates with rounded corners are very common in Ireland.

title: Ireland - Boreens (Grassy Roads) (Plonkit)
description: You will often see a strip of grass in the middle of tiny rural roads. Such roads are called “boreens”. While not unique, these boreens can often be a strong clue in a tough 50-50 between Ireland and the UK.

title: Ireland - Driving Side (Left) (Plonkit)
description: Ireland and the UK drive on the left side of the road.

title: Ireland - Hedgerow Landscape (Plonkit)
description:
Most of Ireland is dominated by a very green, agricultural landscape, with lots of hedgerows next to the roads and dividing the fields.
This type of landscape is also common in many parts of the UK, and can be virtually indistinguishable from Ireland.

title: Ireland - Pole Steps (Plonkit)
description: Both Ireland and the UK use wooden utility poles. Pole steps bolted on the side of the pole are very common. These pole steps are shaped like a series of thin horizontal metal rods.

title: Ireland - Wooden Poles (Plonkit)
description: Both Ireland and the UK occasionally have metal crossbars on their wooden poles.

title: Ireland - Double Yellow Lines (Plonkit)
description: In and around urban areas, you will sometimes encounter double yellow road lines on the sides of marked roads. These indicate a no parking zone, and are also very common in the UK. They are not really found anywhere else in Europe apart from Malta, but landscape should be sufficient to tell it apart.

title: Ireland - Pedestrian Posts (Belisha Beacons) (Plonkit)
description:
Pedestrian crossing signs are somewhat rare in Ireland. They are yellow and diamond-shaped, like other road signs.
Instead of pedestrian signs, you will often see these black and white signposts with a yellow bulb on top.
Note that the UK uses exactly the same signposts.

title: Ireland - Smallcam Coverage (Plonkit)
description: Ireland has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.

title: Ireland - Road Numbering (Regions) (Plonkit)
description:
Irish regional roads have 3-digit road numbers. The first digit of these road numbers gives you a general region within the country (see the infographic).
A good mnemonic to remember the rough location of each region: the numbers go in an anti-clockwise direction around the island, starting in Dublin.
Two important notes:
- There is some overlap between numbers at the borders of each region, as well as some rare exceptions
- Roads starting with 8 or 9 are newer roads that are mostly not limited to a certain region (though about half of the 8s are in the Dublin metro area).

title: Ireland - Phone Area Codes (Plonkit)
description: Irish phone numbers start with a two digit area code. The area codes are grouped geographically by first digit, and are therefore very learnable.

title: Ireland - West Coast Landscape (Plonkit)
description: Ireland’s west coast is defined by a rugged, hilly landscape. Steep hills and low mountains dominate. The neat fields of the east make way for wild grass- and moorlands. The grass often has more brownish and yellow tones to it. Sometimes you will be able to see exposed rocks.

title: Ireland - Donegal Gen 4 Roads (Plonkit)
description:
If a very small rural road has Generation 4 coverage and is located in an unusually hilly landscape, you are likely to be in Donegal.
Note that this meta only applies to the smallest roads: thin, without road lines, and sometimes with grass in the middle. This type of coverage is also not exclusive to Donegal, it is just likely to be there.

title: Ireland - Wicklow Mountains (Plonkit)
description:
One noteworthy area in the east is the Wicklow Mountains, just south of Dublin. They can look deceptively similar to the western coastal mountains. It can be very hard, if not downright impossible to distinguish these two areas.
Two things to look out for:
- You will never see the coast from the Wicklow mountains.
- Like Donegal, its small roads are mostly covered with Generation 4 instead of the Generation 2 that is more typically associated with small roads in the west.

title: Ireland - EV Coverage (Eastern) (Plonkit)
description:
An electrical vehicle (EV) with a Generation 4 camera was used to cover most of Eastern Ireland and parts of the Northwest. The back of the EV is visible in all this coverage: it is grey with a black semicircle.
Note that not all Generation 4 coverage in and around Dublin is made with this car. A considerable amount still has the regular blue Generation 4 car.

title: Ireland - Tabletop Mountains (Plonkit)
description:
In the north of counties Sligo and Leitrim you can find distinctive tabletop mountains.
Note that the mountains in the image are just an example, many of the mountains in this area have the same sort of shape.

title: Ireland - Burren Karst Landscape (Plonkit)
description: The area in and around Burren National Park is characterised by a unique karst landscape consisting of exposed grey limestone rocks.

title: Ireland - Cork Hills (Plonkit)
description: Cork is relatively unique in that it is significantly more hilly than the other big Irish cities.

title: Isle of Man - Overview (Plonkit)
description: Isle of Man is a British Crown dependency, situated between the United Kingdom and Ireland. So for country streaks purposes, it is counted as the United Kingdom.

title: Isle of Man - Low Quality Gen 2 (Plonkit)
description:
Coverage on the Isle of Man is limited to Generation 2.
This camera can be recognized by the lower camera quality and circular blur above and below. Colours will also seem slightly off.

title: Isle of Man - Red Strip Plates (Plonkit)
description: Similar to the United Kingdom, the Isle of Man uses white front licence plates with yellow rears, but with a red strip on the left.

title: Isle of Man - Farmland Landscape (Plonkit)
description: The general landscape on the Isle of Man consists of hilly farmland, and narrow roads passing through them.

title: Isle of Man - Whitewashed Houses (Plonkit)
description: Houses with whitewashed walls and entrance walls are a common sight, similar to Ireland.

title: Isle of Man - Striped Kerbs (Plonkit)
description: Striped kerbs can sometimes be seen along main roads.

title: Isle of Man - Urban Blue Bollards (Plonkit)
description: These blue bollards can commonly be found in urban areas.

title: Isle of Man - Gorse Plants (Plonkit)
description: Gorse plants (or Ulex), which can be recognized by their bright yellow flowers, are very common on the Isle of Man.

title: Isle of Man - Hilly Landscape (Plonkit)
description: Isle of Man is generally quite hilly, with a few exceptions.

title: Isle of Man - Northern Flats vs Southern Mountains (Plonkit)
description: Northern Isle of Man is very flat in comparison to the rest of the island. Usually, there are mountains visible to the south.

title: Isle of Man - Roof Smudge (South) (Plonkit)
description: A ‘twig smudge’ can be seen on the left side of the camera lens in southern Isle of Man.

title: Isle of Man - Douglas Terraced Houses (Plonkit)
description: Douglas, the capital and largest town on the Isle of Man, can be recognized by the rows of terraced houses, with a higher population density.

title: Isle of Man - Laxey Valley (Plonkit)
description: Laxey is a town located in a northwest-southeast valley.

title: Isle of Man - Blue Base Lamps (Plonkit)
description: This generic lamp design with a blue base and a small blue sticker can be found on most of the island, except for around Douglas, and some parts northeast and south. In addition, the top 2 letters can be used to narrow your location down to 1 of the 21 parishes.

title: Isle of Man - Green Lamps (Ramsey) (Plonkit)
description: All green lamps are commonly found in Ramsey and Castletown, as well as more rarely in the Malew, Santon, and Garff parishes.

title: Isle of Man - White Sticker Lamps (Douglas) (Plonkit)
description: A small white sticker with 2 green numbers will be present on lamps in Douglas.

title: Isle of Man - Yellow Sticker Lamps (Onchan) (Plonkit)
description: A small yellow sticker is present on lamps in southern Onchan. The 2 letters are the initials of the road name. E.g. ‘SD’ for Sunningdale Drive.

title: Isle of Man - Ramsey Signs (Coat of Arms) (Plonkit)
description: Many street signs in Ramsey feature the oval shaped coat of arms.

title: Isle of Man - Port Erin Signs (Plonkit)
description: The coat of arms is placed above the text on many signs in Port Erin.

title: Isle of Man - Ronaldsway Airport (Plonkit)
description: The Ronaldsway Airport can be recognized by the large, flat and open field with a boundary fence.

title: Isle of Man - Peel Castle (Plonkit)
description: The Peel castle, sitting atop an island, can unsurprisingly, be seen in Peel.

title: Italy - Short Front Plates (Plonkit)
description: Contrary to most European licence plates, Italian plates have blue strips on either side of the plate. Furthermore, the front plate is distinctly shorter than most European plates, which in combination with the two strips, makes it unique.

title: Italy - Black Top Bollards (Plonkit)
description: Italian bollards are triangular in shape, and white with a black top. They have a red front and a white rear reflector.

title: Italy - Solid White Outer Lines (Plonkit)
description: One of the most common types of Italian road lines are white solid outer lines with no middle line. This is generally less common in other Mediterranean countries.

title: Italy - Italian Language (Plonkit)
description: Italian is the most spoken language in Italy. It uses many double consonants, and typically has a very large number of i’s. You can also find ì, é and à. Most words will end with a vowel.

title: Italy - General Landscape (Plonkit)
description: Italy has a Mediterranean landscape with a lot of agricultural fields on rolling hills, and forested mountain valleys.

title: Italy - Pastel Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Italian architecture mainly consists of pastel coloured stone houses, generally with terracotta roofs. Houses will very commonly have wooden shutters, which will typically be divided in two and open sideways.

title: Italy - Round Concrete Poles (Plonkit)
description: Unlike most Mediterranean countries, Italy features a lot of round concrete poles.

title: Italy - White Sticker Wooden Poles (Plonkit)
description: Wooden poles in Italy will commonly feature a small white pole sticker.

title: Italy - Trident Pole Tops (Plonkit)
description:
The most common pole tops in Italy are concrete trident pole tops.
There are several possible configurations of insulators.The two shown in the image are the most common ones.

title: Italy - Double Guardrails (Plonkit)
description: It is very common to find double guardrails in Italy.

title: Italy - Red Reflector Guardrails (Plonkit)
description: Italian guardrails feature red front reflectors.

title: Italy - Flared Guardrail Ends (Plonkit)
description: Italian guardrails commonly end in this distinct shape. The guardrail gets flatter, wider, and it bends away from the road.

title: Italy - Black Sign Backs (Plonkit)
description: It is very common for the back of Italian road signs to be black, or dark grey.

title: Italy - Blue Directional Signs (Local) (Plonkit)
description: Directional signs are blue with a white arrow. All letters on these signs will be capitalised.

title: Italy - Blue vs Green Highway Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Directional signs in national roads (Strada Statale) are blue with a white and blue border.
Divided highways (Autostrade) have green signs with a white and green border.

title: Italy - Kilometer Markers (Plonkit)
description: Italian kilometre markers are white squares with a roman numeral on top and an arabic numeral on the bottom. The arabic numeral gives you the number of kilometres and the roman numeral gives you the number of hundred metres from the start of the road.

title: Italy - Road Number Prefixes (SS/SR/SP) (Plonkit)
description:
Italian road numbers will normally begin with the letters “SS”, “SR” or “SP”.
The second letter can be used to identify the type of road.
- "S" when it is a State road, so the number is unique within the country.
- "R" when it is a Regional road, so the number is unique to the region.
- "P" when it is a Provincial road, so the number is unique to the province.

title: Italy - Chevron Color Scheme (Plonkit)
description: Italian chevrons are white arrows on a black background.

title: Italy - White Street Signs (Plonkit)
description: Street signs are typically white with a thin blue border and black text.

title: Italy - 5-Stripe Pedestrian Sign (Plonkit)
description: Italian pedestrian signs have five stripes and a basic person without a belt.

title: Italy - Passo Carrabile Signs (Plonkit)
description: These signs, featuring a “no parking”-sign with the text “passo carrabile” are commonly found in urban areas. At the top of these signs you will typically find the municipality (comune) name.

title: Italy - Smallcam Coverage (Plonkit)
description: Italy has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.

title: Italy - Phone Area Codes (Plonkit)
description: Italian area codes follow a pattern where the first digit generally increases to the east, then south.

title: Italy - Regional Flags (Plonkit)
description: Each Italian region has its own unique flag.

title: Italy - South Tyrol German Signs (Plonkit)
description: The region of South Tyrol has a German majority, and as such uses German bilingual signs.

title: Italy - Aosta Valley French Signs (Plonkit)
description: French can be seen on signs in the Aosta Valley. Most notably, street signs often use both the Italian word “via” and the French word “rue”.

title: Italy - Po Valley Haze (Plonkit)
description: The Padan Plain (commonly referred to as Po Valley) can typically be recognized by its complete flatness. The plain has some of the worst air quality in Europe, which has led to much of the coverage having a noticeable haze.

title: Italy - Bari Olive Plantations (Plonkit)
description:
The landscape on the southeastern peninsula surrounding Bari has many olive plantations, which are often seen together with bright rock walls. The dirt in the region typically has a noticeably red colour.
Beware that a similar landscape can also be found in southeastern Sicily.

title: Italy - Alpine Mountains (Plonkit)
description: The alpine region in northern Italy has tall, wide mountain ranges and deep valleys.

title: Italy - Sicilian Landscape (Plonkit)
description: The Sicilian landscape is characterised by an arid, hilly agricultural landscape, often combined with rocky mountains.

title: Italy - Sardinian Granite Rocks (Plonkit)
description: Grey rocks sticking up from the ground are commonly found on Sardinia, particularly in the northeast.

title: Italy - Cacti Distribution (Plonkit)
description: Cacti in Italy are most common in the south, particularly in Sicily, southern Sardinia and the south of Apulia.

title: Italy - Citrus Plantations (Plonkit)
description: Citrus plantations are primarily found on eastern Sicily and the southern tip of Calabria.

title: Italy - Rice Fields (Plonkit)
description: Rice is mainly produced in the western and central parts of Po valley, and less commonly in Sardinia.

title: Italy - Tuscan Brick Architecture (Plonkit)
description: A lot of buildings in and around Tuscany are made of irregular unpainted brown-grey bricks.

title: Italy - Alpine Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Alpine architecture, which typically features large buildings with white stone walls and wooden details, are found in the Alpine region.

title: Italy - Aosta Valley Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Buildings in Aosta Valley are often built with grey uneven bricks, with an Alpine look.

title: Italy - Veneto Shutters (Plonkit)
description: Solid wooden shutters with black metal hinges is a common feature in the northeast of Italy, particularly in Veneto.

title: Italy - Apulian Flat Roofs (Plonkit)
description: Houses in the Apulian region are generally very light coloured, and have flat roofs, typically with two to three floors. The architecture is sometimes reminiscent of the Middle East.

title: Italy - Trulli Houses (Alberobello) (Plonkit)
description: This particular style of roof, called a trullo, is unique to the Itria valley in southeastern Italy. It is particularly common in and around the town of Alberobello.

title: Italy - Slovene Bilingual Signs (Plonkit)
description: Close to the Slovenian border you can find Slovene bilingual signs.

title: Italy - Campione d'Italia Exclave (Plonkit)
description: The Campione d'Italia exclave in Switzerland can be recognized by its low camera, having a long antenna and a flag. There is also a body of water to the west.

title: Italy - Mount Etna (Plonkit)
description: Etna, the tallest volcano in Europe, can be seen rising above the landscape from far away in eastern Sicily.

title: Italy - Mount Vesuvius (Plonkit)
description: The volcano of Vesuvius can often be seen to the south or east from the plains around Naples.

title: Italy - Venice Canals (Plonkit)
description: Venice can typically be recognized by its many canals running through most of the city.

title: Italy - Fucino Plain (Plonkit)
description: Plana del Fùcino is a small plain surrounded by mountains in the middle of Italy with a grid of roads going completely north-to-south.

title: Italy - Pantelleria Volcanic Rock (Plonkit)
description: The island of Pantelleria is a volcanic island southwest of Sicily. Dark volcanic rocks can be seen in the many rock walls of the island, as well as on some houses. It is fairly common to see yellow lichen covering the rocks. The island also has a very large amount of cacti.

title: Italy - Aeolian Islands Landscape (Plonkit)
description:
The Aeolian islands are a volcanic archipelago north of Sicily. Here you will find a mix of volcanic soil and rocks with mediterranean vegetation, like stone pines or olive trees. Like in Sicily, cacti are fairly common.
In the mountains of the islands it is very common to see touristic white villas.

title: Italy - Salina Twin Volcanoes (Plonkit)
description: Within the Aeolian islands, Salina can easily be distinguished from the twin volcanoes forming a valley across the island.

title: Italy - Vulcano Island (Plonkit)
description: Vulcano is perhaps the most easily recognisable of the Aeolian islands, with its volcano having an almost white stripe of dirt following the top of the mountainside. It can typically be spotted from afar on the island.

title: Italy - Favignana Topography (Plonkit)
description:
The island of Favignana has a distinct topography, with mountains running north to south splitting the island in two.
On both sides of the island you will find flat areas, with many rock walls similar to those found in Bari.
Unlike the other islands near Sicily, Favignana is not volcanic.

title: Italy - San Domino Coverage (Plonkit)
description: The island of San Domino only has overcast Generation 2 coverage, which mostly looks quite gloomy.

title: Jersey - Overview (Plonkit)
description: Jersey is a self-governing island territory in the Channel Islands, located off France’s northwestern coast. It is a British Crown Dependency, so for country streaks purposes it is counted as part of the United Kingdom.

title: Jersey - Gen 2 Coverage (Plonkit)
description:
The island is shaped by a unique mix of British and Norman influences. The many winding roads and hedgerows are reminiscent of English country lanes, with tree-covered roads being particularly common. However, due to Jersey’s unique geographical position, most coverage features sunny weather.
All images were taken by a Generation 2 camera.

title: Jersey - License Plates (Plonkit)
description: Jersey licence plates follow the British model, having a long white front and yellow rear plate. In addition, you will notice the island’s red coat of arms on the left, as well as the letter ‘J’ at the beginning of all codes in unblurred plates.

title: Jersey - UK Style Infrastructure (Plonkit)
description: In general, road infrastructure is similar to that found in the United Kingdom. This includes driving on the left, as well as directional signs, chevrons and warning signs. Some of the subtle differences are discussed below.

title: Jersey - French Place Names (Plonkit)
description: Due to its proximity to France, the vast majority of street and locality names contain French words. The island’s traditional language, known as Jèrriais, is closely related to French and appears on some signs.

title: Jersey - Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Similarly, the local architecture shares many characteristics with that of northern France. This includes pastel-coloured walls and dark slate roofs. However, British-style terraced houses are also common.

title: Jersey - Red Granite Buildings (Plonkit)
description: Jersey is home to large reserves of red granite. As a result, it is a popular building material used for the construction of many walls and houses throughout the island.

title: Jersey - Yellow Phone Booths (Plonkit)
description: In contrast to the iconic red booths found on the mainland of the UK, telephone booths in Jersey are uniquely yellow.

title: Jersey - Cornish Palms (Plonkit)
description: Cornish palms (Cordyline australis) can be identified by their distinctive thin trunks and arching leaves. They are commonly used as decorative plants on Jersey.

title: Jersey - Yellow Give Way Lines (Plonkit)
description: Jersey uses yellow give-way lines at intersections.

title: Jersey - Green Lane Signs (Plonkit)
description: Jersey has an extensive network of cycling routes. Most notably, you will find signs referencing the start or end of a “Green Lane”. Blue route markers, containing a map of the island in the centre, are also common.

title: Jersey - Asymmetric Signs (Plonkit)
description: Some road signs are asymmetrically attached to their signposts. This appears to be more prevalent on Jersey than on the British mainland.

title: Jersey - Parish Coat of Arms (Plonkit)
description:
Most street name signs in Jersey are adorned with the coat of arms of the parish in which they are located.
You can click on the graphic to enlarge it.

title: Jersey - St Helier Urban Area (Plonkit)
description: Contrasting with the island’s typically rural look, the area surrounding the capital city of St Helier is more urbanised, featuring taller buildings, narrower streets and a more lively atmosphere.

title: Jersey - Les Mielles Nature Reserve (Plonkit)
description: The Les Mielles Nature Reserve is a vast, treeless expanse located on Jersey’s western coast. Combined with the gentle westward slope and partially overcast coverage, this makes for a very recognisable area.

title: Jersey - Imagery Containing Greenish-purple (Plonkit)
description:
Imagery containing a greenish-purple discolouration can be found in the southwest of the island.
Moreover, this glitch is not unique to Jersey. It can be found in other countries as well.

title: Jersey - Jersey Airport Fence (Plonkit)
description: The roads surrounding Jersey Airport can be recognized thanks to the visible boundary fence.

title: Jersey - La Collette Power Station (Plonkit)
description: The La Collette Power Station is located on a peninsula south of the capital. Its chimney can be seen from various points along the south coast and serves as a useful reference point for pinpointing.

title: Jersey - Victoria Ave (Divided Road) (Plonkit)
description: Victoria Ave runs along the island’s southern coast, immediately west of St Helier. It is the only divided road on Jersey and features a distinct maroon median.

title: Jersey - Southwest Glitch (Plonkit)
description: Imagery containing a greenish-purple discolouration can be found in the southwest of the island.

title: Latvia - License Plates (Plonkit)
description: Latvian licence plates are long and white, with the standard blue European strip on the left.

title: Latvia - Angled Bollards (Plonkit)
description:
Latvian bollards have a thin, slightly curved shape.
They have a rectangular reflector on the front, and two circular reflectors on the back. The reflectors can be white or orange. The black strip is slightly angled. Bollards often have numbers below the front reflector.
!!This infographic shows the main similarities and differences between the bollards of the Baltic and Nordic countries.

title: Latvia - Hook-Shaped Insulators (Plonkit)
description: Latvian poles have distinctive poletops, with hook-shaped insulators, that are arranged in an alternating manner: left-right-left (or vice versa).

title: Latvia - Red-White Chevrons (Plonkit)
description:
Latvia uses white chevrons with red arrows.
!!However, Estonia, Russia and Ukraine use chevrons with the opposite colour scheme: red with white arrows.

title: Latvia - Kilometer Marker Angle (Plonkit)
description:
All Baltic countries use the same blue kilometre marker. However, they can be distinguished from each other by their angle relative to the road.
In Latvia, the marker will be parallel to the road. It only has a number on one side.
For a quick overview of all three Baltic countries, see this infographic.

title: Latvia - Thin Red Sign Border (Plonkit)
description:
Each Baltic country has a slightly different border for its warning and speed signs.
Latvian signs have a thick red border, with a thin white outline around it.

title: Latvia - 5-Stripe Pedestrian Sign (Plonkit)
description:
Latvian pedestrian signs have five stripes, which is unique within the Baltics. Uniquely, the pedestrian has noticeably long legs compared to pedestrian signs in other European countries.
The other two Baltic countries have three stripes on their pedestrian signs.

title: Latvia - Bus Stop Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Latvian bus stop signs have this design.
Most importantly, the bus has five windows. Within the Baltics, this is unique to Latvia. The other two Baltic countries have four windows.

title: Latvia - A-Type Guardrails (Plonkit)
description: Latvia has normal A-type guardrails with white or red reflectors.

title: Latvia - Language Characteristics (Plonkit)
description:
Latvian belongs to the Baltic languages. The other major member of this branch is Lithuanian, to which it is closely related.
Within the Baltic languages, the following letters are unique to Latvian:
- Vowels with a macron (horizontal stripe): Ā Ē Ī.
- Consonants with a small hook: Ģ Ķ Ļ Ņ.

title: Latvia - Street Naming ('Iela') (Plonkit)
description:
The Latvian word for street is iela. This word is unique to Latvian.
Very rarely, you might see ‘gatve’ in Riga (abbreviated as gat.). This word is also the standard word for street in Lithuania (usually abbreviated as g.).

title: Latvia - House Numbers (Plonkit)
description: Latvian house numbers are often shaped like tall rectangles and can be found in several colours.

title: Latvia - Wood & White Brick Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Latvian architecture generally consists of a combination of wood and white brick, typically with somewhat steep corrugated metal roofs. Slightly modern houses with pastel coloured stone walls and houses with a combination of wood with another material, particularly white brick, are also common.

title: Latvia - Directional Signs (Plonkit)
description: Latvian directional signs are blue with white text.

title: Latvia - Red Gen 4 Car (Plonkit)
description: A red generation 4 Google car can be found in Latvia.

title: Latvia - Black Gen 4 Car (Plonkit)
description: A black generation 4 Google car can also be found in Latvia.

title: Latvia - Jelgava Landscape (Plonkit)
description: The area south of Jelgava is characterised by a wide open landscape with considerably less forest and more fields than most of the rest of Latvia.

title: Latvia - Riga Art Nouveau (Plonkit)
description: The historic downtown area of Riga is characterised by majestic art nouveau architecture, that is in places reminiscent of the architecture in Vienna. This is unique within Latvia, and even within the entire Baltics.

title: Latvia - Curved Road Bollards (Plonkit)
description:
Latvian bollards have a thin, slightly curved shape.

They have a rectangular reflector on the front, and two circular reflectors on the back. The reflectors can be white or orange. The black strip is slightly angled. Bollards often have numbers below the front reflector.

title: Latvia - Chevron Color Scheme (Plonkit)
description: Latvia uses white chevrons with red arrows.

title: Liechtenstein - License Plates (Plonkit)
description: Liechtenstein uses black plates with white lettering and a yellow-and-red emblem near the left side. When blurred, the plates will appear grey, with the emblem colours being visible.

title: Liechtenstein - Valley Landscape (Plonkit)
description:
Most coverage in Liechtenstein is situated in a somewhat flat river valley, but with tall mountains in almost every direction. In particular, within this valley, you will almost always be able to see the nearby mountains towering above you to the east. Most of the mountainous coverage is just on the slopes of the mountains, with only a small amount properly in the mountains.
As a result of the flat Rhine River Valley, Liechtenstein has a lot of pastures and other agricultural land.

title: Liechtenstein - Lowcam Coverage (Plonkit)
description:
All coverage in Liechtenstein is low-cam. This means that the camera on the Google car is intentionally set up lower than in most other countries. This can be recognized in two ways:
- The car blur is significantly bigger.
- Roads look wider and objects around you are seen from a lower angle.
Generally, the bigger car blur is the most consistent way to recognize low-cam.

title: Liechtenstein - Cylindrical Bollards (Plonkit)
description:
Liechtenstein uses black-and-white cylindrical bollards with a white or grey reflector and a rounded top. They also often have a blue attachment on the side.
When attached to guardrails, they will use the wedge design instead.

title: Liechtenstein - Green/White Bus Stops (Plonkit)
description: Bus stops in Liechtenstein use a green-and-white design, with a black metallic border around the sign. The phrase LIEMOBIL is written at the top.

title: Liechtenstein - Directional Signs (Plonkit)
description: Like Switzerland, directional signs in Liechtenstein are generally white (smaller roads) or blue (bigger roads), and they have a pointed arrowhead, with a contrasting colour.

title: Liechtenstein - 7-Stripe Pedestrian Sign (Plonkit)
description: Liechtenstein pedestrian signs have seven stripes. The signs also have an oddly tall rectangle.

title: Liechtenstein - Yellow/Black Road Separators (Plonkit)
description: You can find these yellow-and-black striped road separators, with a rounded top, and a Lego-like knob on the top. They have 3 stripes of both colours, with yellow on the bottom.

title: Liechtenstein - Grey Sign Borders (Plonkit)
description: Road signs in Liechtenstein commonly have a round, grey metal border around them.

title: Liechtenstein - Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Architecture in Liechtenstein is a blend of traditional Alpine styles and more modern buildings, especially in the bigger cities.

title: Liechtenstein - Triesenberg Slope (Plonkit)
description: Triesenberg and its surroundings are a fairly densely populated area on the slope of the mountains just east of the Rhine River Valley, which can often be seen below to the west.

title: Liechtenstein - Eastern Mountains (Plonkit)
description: Mountains can be seen all around in the coverage east of the mountain ridge that cuts through Liechtenstein.

title: Liechtenstein - Ruggell Ridge (Plonkit)
description: Around Ruggell, there is a small, forested ridgeline to the south. This is a big contrast to the towering mountains seen elsewhere.

title: Liechtenstein - Mauren Hills (Plonkit)
description: Around Mauren, you can see the aforementioned ridge to the north, but this side of the hills is much more developed and urban. And to the south and southeast, you will see the much bigger mountains usually seen to the east.

title: Liechtenstein - Rolling Hills (Bendern) (Plonkit)
description: There is a set of rolling hills that run from Bendern, northeast, to the Austrian border. The rest of Liechtenstein is either very flat or in the mountains.

title: Liechtenstein - Swiss Peaks View (Plonkit)
description: In the flat area west of Balzers, with the northeast-oriented gridded roads, to the North/Northwest, you can often see two rocky peaks on the Swiss side.

title: Liechtenstein - Vaduz Bus Stops (Red) (Plonkit)
description: Unlike the rest of Liechtenstein, Vaduz sometimes uses red bus stop signs.

title: Liechtenstein - Balzers Bus Stops (Black) (Plonkit)
description: Unlike the rest of Liechtenstein, Balzers sometimes uses black bus stop signs.

title: Liechtenstein - Blue Signs (White Border) (Plonkit)
description: Blue street signs with a thin white border will place you either in the south of Liechtenstein or in the north around Bandern.

title: Liechtenstein - Blue Signs (No Border) (Plonkit)
description: Blue street signs that don’t have an outline are found in Eschen.

title: Liechtenstein - Black Signs (Plonkit)
description: Flat black signs are found in eastern Liechtenstein.

title: Liechtenstein - Schaan Signs (Plonkit)
description: Black signs with a white border and embossed letters can be found in Schaan.

title: Liechtenstein - Brown Signs (White Border) (Plonkit)
description: These brown street signs with a font reminiscent of traditional German typefaces, along with a white border, are found in Vaduz and the northern towns.

title: Liechtenstein - Ruggell Arrow Signs (Plonkit)
description: Brown street signs that have an arrow design are unique to Ruggell.

title: Liechtenstein - Planken Signs (Plonkit)
description: Browns signs which have a more ‘generic’ font will place you in Planken.

title: Liechtenstein - Maels Cliff (Plonkit)
description: This steep rocky cliff with trees at its base and on the top can be seen in and around Mäls.

title: Liechtenstein - Steg Lakes (Plonkit)
description: The only lakes in Liechtenstein are located just south of Steg, near the middle of the mountains.

title: Lithuania - License Plates (Plonkit)
description: Lithuanian licence plates are long and white, with the standard blue European strip on the left.

title: Lithuania - Road Bollards (Plonkit)
description:
Lithuanian bollards are wedge-shaped.
They have an orange reflector on the front, and a white reflector on the back. Both reflectors are rectangular. You may find this thin version as well.
This infographic shows the main similarities and differences between the bollards of the Baltic and Nordic countries.

title: Lithuania - Square Concrete Poles (Plonkit)
description: Lithuanian poles are usually square and concrete, and often feature a diagonal support beam.

title: Lithuania - Trident Pole Tops (Plonkit)
description:
Pictured here are some typical Lithuanian poletops.
- They often have short horizontal rods, on which the insulators are placed.
- In some poletops, the insulators are arranged in a trident-like shape, with one on top, and two on each side.
Note that these poletops are not unique to Lithuania: they can also be found in the other post-Soviet countries.

title: Lithuania - Red-White Chevrons (Plonkit)
description:
Lithuania uses white chevrons with red arrows. The small single chevrons (pictured here) usually have a red outline on the edge of the sign.
!!However, Estonia, Russia and Ukraine use chevrons with the opposite colour scheme: red with white arrows.

title: Lithuania - Kilometer Marker Angle (Plonkit)
description:
All Baltic countries use the same blue kilometre marker. However, they can be distinguished from each other by their angle relative to the road.
In Lithuania, the marker will be at a 45° angle towards the road. The sign itself has an L-shape.
For a quick overview of all three Baltic countries, see this infographic.

title: Lithuania - Thin Red Sign Border (Plonkit)
description:
Each Baltic country has a slightly different border for its warning and speed signs.
Lithuanian signs have a relatively thin red border, with a thin white outline around it.

title: Lithuania - Road Guardrails (Plonkit)
description: Lithuania has normal A-type guardrails with orange reflectors.

title: Lithuania - Lithuanian Pedestrian Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Lithuanian pedestrian signs have 3 stripes. The shape of the pedestrian has a relatively low level of detail.
!!Latvian pedestrian signs have 5 stripes.

title: Lithuania - Bus Stop Designs (Plonkit)
description:
Lithuanian bus stop signs have this design.
The bus has four windows. This is mostly useful to distinguish it from the Latvian bus stop sign, which has five windows.
Note however, that Estonia has the same bus stop signs as Lithuania.

title: Lithuania - Language Characteristics (Plonkit)
description:
Lithuanian belongs to the Baltic languages. The other major member of this branch is Latvian, to which it is closely related.
Within the Baltic languages, the following letters are unique to Lithuanian:
- Vowels with small hooks: Ą Ę Į Ų.
- Ė with a single dot.
- Y (also in Estonian, but only in loan words).

title: Lithuania - Capital City Features (Plonkit)
description:
The Lithuanian word for street is gatve, often abbreviated as g. on signs and Google Maps.
This word is almost entirely unique to Lithuanian. However, very rarely, you might see ‘gatve’ (abbreviated as gat.) in the Latvian capital of Riga.

title: Lithuania - Place Names ('-ai') (Plonkit)
description: Many Lithuanian place names end in -ai.

title: Lithuania - Local Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Lithuanian architecture primarily consists of light coloured brick buildings, usually with somewhat steep corrugated metal roofs. Wooden buildings are also fairly common, however less so than in Estonia. Pastel painted stone buildings are somewhat common, especially in newer suburbs.

title: Lithuania - Directional Signs (Plonkit)
description: Lithuanian directional signs are blue with white text.

title: Lithuania - Historical Site (Plonkit)
description: Lithuania's historical state flag, known as the Vytis, depicts a mounted knight on a dark red background. It can sometimes be seen on both private and public buildings.

title: Lithuania - Agricultural Area (Plonkit)
description: Lithuania has less forest cover than the other two Baltic countries. As a result, the landscape appears more open and agricultural. Your mileage may vary depending on the round however, so use this meta with some caution.

title: Lithuania - License Plates (Plonkit)
description:
In Generation 3 coverage, you will often see random small blurs. These blurs look similar to the ones that are used to blur out licence plates or faces, but instead they cover seemingly random parts of the image – often on direction signs.
!!These random blurs are not typically found in Estonia or Latvia.

title: Lithuania - Lithuania Features (Plonkit)
description: A black generation 4 Google car can be found in Lithuania.

title: Lithuania - Lithuania Features (Plonkit)
description: A red generation 4 Google car can also be found in Lithuania.

title: Lithuania - Hilly Terrain (Plonkit)
description: Lithuania is overall a fairly flat country, with no hills over 300 metres. However, you can sometimes distinguish the hilly areas from the more flat areas. The biggest hills are in the southeast, with some hills in the central part of the west.

title: Lithuania - Metal Poles (Plonkit)
description:
Metal pole tags are predominantly found in the eastern part of the country.
For more information on Lithuanian pole stickers and car metas, please see this document.

title: Lithuania - Pine Forests (Plonkit)
description:
The Curonian Spit is a long thin sand-dune spit) south of Klaipeda, that separates the Curonian Lagoon from the Baltic Sea. The main road on this spit, road 167, has a recognizable combination of landscape and road direction:
- The road runs in an approximate north-south direction and has Generation 4 coverage.
The road is surrounded on all sides by forest with many Baltic pines. In many places, you will see slightly windswept trees (visible in the example image).

title: Lithuania - Curonian Spit (Architecture) (Plonkit)
description: On the Curonian Spit you can also find wooden, and often red, Scandinavian looking houses.

title: Lithuania - Polish Bilingual Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Rarely, you can see bilingual signs with Polish language in a small area southeast of Lithuania.
Note that this is by no means very common, but it can help with getting very close guesses if you do see bilingual Polish-Lithuanian signs in an otherwise obvious Lithuanian setting.

title: Lithuania - Wedge-Shaped Bollards (Plonkit)
description:
Lithuanian bollards are wedge-shaped.

They have an orange reflector on the front, and a white reflector on the back. Both reflectors are rectangular. You may find this thin version as well.

title: Lithuania - Chevron Color Scheme (Plonkit)
description: Lithuania uses white chevrons with red arrows. The small single chevrons (pictured here) usually have a red outline on the edge of the sign.

title: Lithuania - 3-Stripe Pedestrian Sign (Plonkit)
description: Lithuanian pedestrian signs have 3 stripes. The shape of the pedestrian has a relatively low level of detail.

title: Lithuania - License Plates (Plonkit)
description: In Generation 3 coverage, you will often see random small blurs. These blurs look similar to the ones that are used to blur out licence plates or faces, but instead they cover seemingly random parts of the image – often on direction signs.

title: Luxembourg - Luxembourg Uses Long (Plonkit)
description:
Luxembourg uses long yellow plates with a blue strip on the left.
Since Luxembourg is a small country, foreign cars with white plates are somewhat common.
- The Netherlands has yellow plates front and rear.
- The UK has yellow rear plates.
- Some pre-2009 French cars have yellow rear plates.

title: Luxembourg - Striped Bollards (Plonkit)
description:
Bollards are black and white. They are wedge-shaped and have grey reflectors. Some have a distinctive indent in the lower half.
The bollards of Belgium, the Netherlands and France look very different.

title: Luxembourg - Yellow-Black Chevrons (Plonkit)
description:
Chevrons are black with yellow arrows. You may also rarely come across blue and yellow chevrons.
The only other European countries with this colour scheme tend to have wildly different landscapes: Iceland, Norway, Finland, Ireland, and Portugal.

title: Luxembourg - Utility Poles (Plonkit)
description:
Poles with poletops shaped like upside-down tridents are the most common type of pole in Luxembourg.
In addition, you can find a variety of other poletops.

title: Luxembourg - Gen 2 Coverage (Plonkit)
description:
Almost all coverage in Luxembourg is either Generation 2 or Generation 4.
Generation 3 is rare, but does exist.

title: Luxembourg - Multilingual Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Luxembourg is a highly multilingual country. It has three administrative languages: Luxembourgish, French, and German.
French is the language that is mostly used for public communication. Road signs and advertisements are usually in French.
Presence of German on signs is less common compared to French, but certainly not non-existent.

title: Luxembourg - Luxembourgish Language (Plonkit)
description:
Luxembourgish is closely related to German and can look very similar. Like German, it uses umlauts (dots over vowels). In addition, it uses a fair amount of double vowels, and sometimes an é with an accent.
Most town names have their origin in Luxembourgish, German, or both.

title: Luxembourg - Directional Signs (Yellow) (Plonkit)
description:
Directional signs are yellow with a thin black outline. Town names are written in uppercase. The signs have a pointed tip. They are completely surrounded by a frame, making them very recognizable.
Some directional signs feature road numbers:
- Regional road numbers have 1 or 2 digits and a red box.
- Local road numbers have 3 digits and a yellow box.

title: Luxembourg - Town Entrance Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Town entrance signs are also yellow and surrounded by a frame.
Most of these signs have bilingual versions of the town name. They frequently have the road number on the top, along with a speed limit sign.

title: Luxembourg - Sign Frames (Plonkit)
description: The frames mentioned in the previous two tips are also commonly found on a lot of other road infrastructure.

title: Luxembourg - White Signposts (Plonkit)
description: Almost all Luxembourgish road signs will be supported by a white signpost.

title: Luxembourg - Blue Street Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Street signs are almost always short and usually have a white background. The exact designs vary from town to town.
A very common design is the one pictured on the left in the example image, with slanted blue corners.
In addition, Dutch street signs almost always have a blue background and tend to be much longer than they are tall.

title: Luxembourg - Blue/White Post Reflectors (Plonkit)
description: Some signposts have this bulky, round reflector with blue and white markings.

title: Luxembourg - Pedestrian Signs Have (Plonkit)
description: Pedestrian signs have 5 vertical stripes.

title: Luxembourg - Bus Stop Designs (Plonkit)
description: Bus stop signs are blue and always have this exact design. The bus has six windows.

title: Luxembourg - Rolling Hills (Plonkit)
description: Almost all of Luxembourg’s landscape consists of green rolling hills, with a patchwork of agriculture and forests.

title: Luxembourg - Slate Roof Architecture (Plonkit)
description:
Houses tend to have dark slate roofs.
Walls and windows tend to be plain and undecorated. Walls are usually painted white, grey, or pastel colours.

title: Luxembourg - Capital City Features (Plonkit)
description:
Local road numbers have three digits. They are geographically clustered by first digit. The first digits range from 1-3.
- 1xx is found in the southern half.
- 2xx is found in and around the capital.
- 3xx is found in the northern half.

title: Luxembourg - Northern Hills (Plonkit)
description: The north of the country is hillier and has an overall higher elevation than the south.

title: Luxembourg - Southeast Vineyards (Plonkit)
description: Vineyards are primarily found in the southeast of the country.

title: Luxembourg - Gen 3 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: Some of Luxembourg City’s downtown area was covered by a Generation 3 urban trekker. Occasionally, the trekker’s sunglasses and greying hair can be seen.

title: Luxembourg - License Plates (Plonkit)
description:
Luxembourg uses long yellow plates with a blue strip on the left.

Since Luxembourg is a small country, foreign cars with white plates are somewhat common.

title: Luxembourg - Striped Bollards (Plonkit)
description: Bollards are black and white. They are wedge-shaped and have grey reflectors. Some have a distinctive indent in the lower half.

title: Luxembourg - Yellow-Black Chevrons (Plonkit)
description: Chevrons are black with yellow arrows. You may also rarely come across blue and yellow chevrons.

title: Luxembourg - Blue Street Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Street signs are almost always short and usually have a white background. The exact designs vary from town to town.

A very common design is the one pictured on the left in the example image, with slanted blue corners.

title: Madeira - Portuguese Infrastructure (Plonkit)
description: Since Madeira is an autonomous region of Portugal, you will often come across various types of Portuguese infrastructure, such as poles and chevrons.

title: Madeira - Mountainous Landscape (Plonkit)
description: Madeira is a very mountainous and semi-tropical island.

title: Madeira - Eucalyptus Forests (Plonkit)
description: Similar to continental Portugal, Madeira has a lot of eucalyptus forests, which can sometimes look deceptively like the mainland.

title: Madeira - Hydrangeas (Plonkit)
description: Hydrangeas can occasionally be seen.

title: Madeira - African Lilies (Plonkit)
description: African lilies (Agapanthus praecox) are very common in Madeira. They can be recognized by their long grassy leaves and round flower clusters at the end of a long stem. The most common colours are white and blue.

title: Madeira - Terrace Farming (Plonkit)
description: Due to the lack of flat terrain, terrace farming is extensively practised on the island. Stone walls are used to separate the individual plateaus.

title: Madeira - Ferns (Plonkit)
description: Ferns are very common throughout the island.

title: Madeira - Architecture Colors (Plonkit)
description: Houses are mainly painted white, grey, or pastel colours such as yellow and pink. In addition, the red tile roofs will often be in a good condition.

title: Madeira - Concrete Barriers (Plonkit)
description: Concrete block barriers, usually painted white, are often found along roads.

title: Madeira - Bus Stop Signs (Plonkit)
description: Bus stops signs on Madeira follow a unique black, white and yellow colour scheme.

title: Madeira - Yellow Taxis (Blue Stripe) (Plonkit)
description: Taxis on Madeira are yellow with a blue stripe running along the sides of the car.

title: Madeira - Stone Bollards (Plonkit)
description: Madeira commonly uses small and unique stone bollards with a red reflector. They are either cuboidal or cylindrical in shape.

title: Madeira - Guardrails (Yellow/Black) (Plonkit)
description: Madeira sometimes uses yellow-and black guardrails on its mountain roads.

title: Madeira - Highway Speed Signs (Plonkit)
description: These speed limit signs are unique to Madeira and can be found on its highways.

title: Madeira - Low Altitude Clouds (Plonkit)
description: Low altitude clouds are typical on the island, and are often seen on street view.

title: Madeira - Foggy Coverage (Plonkit)
description: Foggy coverage is quite common.

title: Madeira - Tunnels (Plonkit)
description: As a result of the island’s mountainous terrain, tunnels are very common.

title: Madeira - Green Bridge Railings (Plonkit)
description: On bridges you will often find railings painted dark green.

title: Madeira - Striped Signposts (Plonkit)
description: Signposts on Madeira are often striped.

title: Madeira - Free Roaming Cows (Plonkit)
description: You can sometimes find free roaming cows on high-altitude roads on the island, as well as warning signs for those cows. The cows will typically be brown with white spots, contrary to the Azores, where the cows will typically be black and white.

title: Madeira - Low Quality Camera (Plonkit)
description:
Google used a weird, low-quality camera on Madeira, commonly known as the official Ari (or "shitcam"). It has a wide circular car blur and makes the image appear rather gloomy. On Madeira, you will often see the unblurred back of a white car.
A good map will usually not include this coverage, but it is good to be aware of its existence, in order not to be caught off-guard.

title: Madeira - Banana Plantations (South) (Plonkit)
description: The majority of banana plantations are found in the south.

title: Madeira - Central-West Plateau (Plonkit)
description: The centre-west of the island is home to an elevated plateau. It can be recognized by the unusual flatness, misty coverage, and the presence of wind turbines.

title: Madeira - Eastern Mountains (East of Plateau) (Plonkit)
description: The road east of the plateau can be recognized by its unique mountain formations and the black-and-yellow guardrail on the side of the road.

title: Madeira - Eastern Tip (Arid) (Plonkit)
description: The eastern tip of the island is very arid with little to no vegetation.

title: Madeira - ER211 Road (Dark Pavement) (Plonkit)
description: The ER211 can be recognized by the dark pavement combined with its exposed brownish soil.

title: Madeira - Pico Areeiro (Radar Station) (Plonkit)
description: Pico Areeiro is the second highest mountain on the island, and the highest with coverage. It can be recognized by its view over most of the island, and the white radar station at the top.

title: Madeira - Penha d'Aguia Rock (Plonkit)
description: The Penha d'Águia is located in northeastern Madeira, isolated on an elevated hill.

title: Madeira - Airport Pillars (Plonkit)
description: The Cristiano Ronaldo International Airport is located in eastern Madeira. The north of it is built on these numerous concrete pillars.

title: Madeira - Cascata dos Anjos (Plonkit)
description: Cascata dos Anjos is situated in the southwest and is a popular location on the island. It is a 100-metre-high waterfall, which cascades onto the road below.

title: Madeira - Ribeira da Janela Rocks (Plonkit)
description: The islands of Ribeira de Janela, located in the northwest, are a famous photographer spot with their vertical, jagged shape.

title: Madeira - Porto Moniz Rocks (Plonkit)
description: These dark, sharp rock formations with an island in the background are found in Porto Moniz in the northwest.

title: Malta - Driving Side (Left) (Plonkit)
description: Malta drives on the left.

title: Malta - Short Plates (Plonkit)
description: Like most of Europe, Maltese licence plates have a blue strip on the left. However, unlike most of Europe, short plates are very common.

title: Malta - Dry Hilly Landscape (Plonkit)
description: The general landscape of Malta consists of slightly hilly dry agricultural fields. Many roads are also only 1 or 2 lanes wide, due to the island’s size. Having a mediterranean climate, cacti and various dry shrubs can be seen.

title: Malta - Limestone Rock Walls (Plonkit)
description: Limestone rock walls are extremely common in Malta. This alone is usually enough to determine that you are in Malta.

title: Malta - Limestone Architecture (Plonkit)
description: The vast majority of buildings in Malta consist of low storey buildings, with white to beige coloured walls. Buildings made of limestone are also fairly common.

title: Malta - Traditional Balconies (Plonkit)
description: This style of traditional covered balconies is very common on Maltese buildings. They are often painted in bright colours.

title: Malta - Street Naming ('Triq') (Plonkit)
description: The Maltese word for street is “triq”, which can be seen on almost every street sign.

title: Malta - Bus Stop Signs (Plonkit)
description: Bus stops are a common sight in Malta. They may sometimes have useful information as to where you are.

title: Malta - Double Yellow Lines (Plonkit)
description: Like the UK and Ireland, Malta uses these distinctive double yellow no parking lines.

title: Malta - English Language (Plonkit)
description: English is the primary language of Malta.

title: Malta - Maltese Language (Plonkit)
description:
Apart from English it is also common to see the Maltese language. Maltese uses the Latin script, but with unique letters, which include:
- Ċ ċ
- Ġ ġ
- Ħ ħ
- Ż ż

title: Malta - Stone Barriers (Gozo) (Plonkit)
description: Regular metal guardrails are rare on Gozo Island. Low stone barriers are more common instead.

title: Malta - Gozo Bus Numbers (300s) (Plonkit)
description: Uniquely, all bus routes on Gozo Island are in the 300s. These can be quite hard to see, meaning they are most useful in moving games.

title: Malta - Valletta Blue Signs (Plonkit)
description: These blue signs are unique to Valletta.

title: Malta - Gozo Ferry Trekker (Plonkit)
description: This trekker on a ship that is painted white and blue can be seen between the main island and Gozo Island.

title: Monaco - Location Overview (Plonkit)
description: Monaco is a European microstate on the French Riviera, a few kilometres west of the border with Italy.

title: Monaco - Urban Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Monaco is a rich and densely populated city state, with a Mediterranean feel to it. The architecture is similar to cities in southern France and northern Italy, but more luxurious. You will see a lot of apartment buildings, neoclassical details, and pastel colours. There are essentially no rural areas.

title: Monaco - License Plates (Plonkit)
description:
Monaco’s licence plates are short and lack the blue strip.
You will still see a lot of normal French plates around, however. These French vehicles often still have the old yellow back plates, due to how old the Generation 2 coverage is.

title: Monaco - Hilly Landscape (Plonkit)
description: Monaco is a hilly country. The very few areas that are not built up show mediterranean vegetation.

title: Monaco - Palm Trees (Plonkit)
description: Planted palm trees are common.

title: Monaco - Tunnel Coverage (Plonkit)
description: There is a lot of coverage inside tunnels.

title: Monaco - Parked Mopeds (Plonkit)
description: Rows of parked mopeds are a common sight around Monaco’s streets.

title: Monaco - Harbour Boat Trekker (Plonkit)
description:
In the harbour, there is an extensive Generation 3 trekker on a boat. The Google employee’s brown hair and sunglasses are visible. You can see Monaco’s skyline and the hills beyond it. There are a lot of expensive yachts around.
This trekker shows up a lot in the official competitive game modes, so it is worth remembering.

title: Montenegro - License Plates (Plonkit)
description: Montenegro uses the standard European plate with a blue strip, and the Montenegro coat of arms on a red circle. The red circle is visible through the blur.

title: Montenegro - All Generation 4 (Plonkit)
description: All Generation 4 coverage in Montenegro was taken using a “smallcam” camera, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.

title: Montenegro - Mountainous Landscape (Plonkit)
description: Montenegro is a small, mountainous country. Inland mountains are lush and green, while most coastal mountains have distinct exposed, light coloured rock. Most roads are also only 1 or 2 lanes wide.

title: Montenegro - Black Top Bollards (Plonkit)
description: The most common bollard is white with a red reflector on the front and a white one on the back. The bollard also has a black top.

title: Montenegro - Chevron Color Scheme (Plonkit)
description: Montenegro uses black on white or red on yellow chevrons.

title: Montenegro - Rusted Guardrails (Plonkit)
description: Guardrails in Montenegro are often rusted.

title: Montenegro - A-Type & B-Type Guardrails (Plonkit)
description: Montenegro is the only Balkan country where you’ll commonly see both A-type and B-type guardrails.

title: Montenegro - Utility Poles (Plonkit)
description: Montenegro uses simple round concrete or wooden poles.

title: Montenegro - Gen 3 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: ‘Rifts’ can uncommonly be seen in Montenegrin generation 3 coverage, due to poor stitching.

title: Montenegro - Gen 3 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: Although rifts are common in generation 3 Montenegro coverage, coastal rounds will almost never have them. By the coast, there will be a short antenna with no rifts. There will be a long antenna with rifts inland.

title: Montenegro - Northern Valleys (Plonkit)
description: Green, agricultural valleys with deforested hills to make way for farmland are most commonly seen in the north.

title: Montenegro - Bay of Kotor (Plonkit)
description: The Bay of Kotor has a touristy and populated feel to it, with many people dressed in swimwear. A distinct steep, rocky ridge can also be seen.

title: Montenegro - Dry Landscape (Podgorica) (Plonkit)
description: Dry mountains with a lack of trees are seen around Podgorica, and to the south of it. Vineyards are also commonly seen in this region.

title: Montenegro - Pine Forests (Plonkit)
