description: While houses in Sweden are mostly very colourful, on the west coast they are commonly much lighter. There are an especially large number of white and light yellow houses along the coast between Gothenburg and the Norwegian border.

title: Sweden - West Coast Sheds (Plonkit)
description: Dense rows of very small red sheds are commonly found in coastal towns on the northern west coast.

title: Sweden - Dalarna Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Central Dalarna has a strong tradition of wooden craftsmanship, and as a result much of the architecture has a unique, picturesque look to it. Most commonly, you may find red timbered houses, portals made of logs, and so-called härbren which have a very distinct design.

title: Sweden - Hälsingland Has Many (Plonkit)
description: Hälsingland has many big, mostly red, farmhouses. They are characterised by many large windows, 2–3 floors, and the front facade being long and grand-looking. Barns can also be seen having an unusual amount of windows in the region.

title: Sweden - Leaning Sheds (Plonkit)
description: Along the northern coast you will commonly encounter agricultural sheds which are either octagonal or rectangular, with the walls noticeably leaning outwards. They will typically be made out of red-painted logs.

title: Sweden - Gotland Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Houses on Gotland are commonly made of limestone and often have a dirty-looking white facade. Churches on Gotland are very distinct looking, with either grey walls or white walls with grey corners, a large portal around the door and small windows typically divided in two by a pillar.

title: Sweden - Öland Stone (Plonkit)
description: This type of uneven stone brick is typically found in houses and rock walls on Öland, and less commonly in rock walls on Gotland.

title: Sweden - Regional Bus Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Each administrative region in Sweden has at least one, and in many cases several, bus stop signs which are unique to that region.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Sweden - Bus Stop Designs (Plonkit)
description:
Many regions have their own distinct type of bus shelters, which may either replace or complement the bus stop signs. This image contains the ones which are most common and easily recognizable.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Sweden - Road Numbers (Plonkit)
description:
Besides the European highways, there are two types of numbered roads in Sweden, national roads (9-99) and regional roads (100-404). Numbers typically increase the further northeast you get. These maps are only approximate, since some roads go across many of the regions shown.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Sweden - Snowmobile Trail Crosses (Plonkit)
description: Small red crosses marking snowmobile trails can be found throughout the northern half of the country.

title: Sweden - Dalarna Red Roads (Plonkit)
description: Many roads in western Dalarna and nearby regions have a very noticeable red colour.

title: Sweden - Umeå Green Poles (Plonkit)
description: Green snow poles can occasionally be found in the area surrounding Umeå.

title: Sweden - Wedge-Shaped Bollards (Plonkit)
description: Wedge-shaped bollards, similar to those found in Germany, are most common in the southern regions of the country.

title: Sweden - Black-Top Bollards (Plonkit)
description: Cylindrical bollards, with a completely horizontal black section near the top, are most commonly found near the west coast and in Värmland and southern Dalarna.

title: Sweden - Flat/Angled Bollards (Plonkit)
description:
Flat bollards, or cylindrical bollards with a black rectangle containing the reflector are most commonly found on major roads in the northern half of the country.
Beware that one type of flat bollards can look similar to the cylindrical bollards from the last tip, however the black section here is not horizontal.

title: Sweden - Skåne Small Bollards (Plonkit)
description: These small white bollards with either a blue or a red strip near the top can be found in the countryside of Skåne.

title: Sweden - Railway Crossing ID (Plonkit)
description: The backside of railway crossing signs have a yellow sticker with a 5-digit ID number. The first digit indicates the region, and it predominantly increases to the northeast.

title: Sweden - Place Name Endings (Plonkit)
description:
Some place name endings are limited to a certain region. This map shows some common and useful endings.
Place names are not limited to just villages and towns: local farmsteads and other geographical points of interest are also included.
The distributions shown on the maps are not 100% definite. Some exceptions exist.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Sweden - Sámi Bilingual Signs (Plonkit)
description: Sámi bilingual signs can be found inland in the northern parts of Sweden.

title: Sweden - Meänkieli Language Closely (Plonkit)
description: Meänkieli is a language closely related to Finnish, which is found close to the Finnish border. One of the most common occurrences on signage is for river names, which will end in “väylä”. It is also possible to find trilingual signs with both Meänkieli and Sámi.

title: Sweden - Blue Stripe Car (Plonkit)
description: Along the Swedish west coast, and in Skåne, you may find a white Google car with a blue stripe on the back.

title: Sweden - Area Code Map (Plonkit)
description:
The first 3-4 (2 in Stockholm) digits of landline phone numbers in Sweden are the area code. The map shows the first two digits in every region. Within the regions, the third and fourth digit of area codes typically increase to the northeast.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Sweden - E10 Borders (Plonkit)
description: The E10 between Kiruna and the Norwegian border is a major road which can be recognised by the vegetation mainly consisting of small birches, occasionally with some pines strewn in, combined with snow covered mountains, which can typically be seen in the distant west close to Kiruna, and in all directions when you approach the border. A major lake can also be seen to the north on the western half of the road.

title: Sweden - Road 99 Forest (Plonkit)
description:
The northern section of road 99 can usually be recognized by its grey sandy ground with brown-green moss, the noticeable ditch following most of the road and its fairly low, dense forest with a mixture of birches, pines and spruces.
Beware that the most recent coverage on much of the road was taken during early spring, which makes some of these features harder to recognise.

title: Sweden - Ritsem Road (Plonkit)
description: The road to Ritsem can generally be recognised by having a large lake following it on the south, combined with having some of the most dramatic mountains seen on Street View in the country. The road is small and without roadlines, but still fairly well-paved. It is covered both in summer and in early spring.

title: Sweden - Wilderness Road (Plonkit)
description: Most mountain roads in Sweden have been built below the treeline, resulting in small trees being visible on almost all coverage. The only paved road in Sweden above the treeline, with no visible trees, can be found on the border between Jämtland and Västerbotten, near the Norwegian border. The coverage was taken during fall, giving the limited vegetation a yellowish brown colour.

title: Sweden - Flatruet Road (Plonkit)
description: The highest altitude public road in Sweden, which is a dirt road going straight over a treeless mountain plateau, was covered in Generation 4 on a cloudy day during summer.

title: Sweden - Kiruna Mountains (Plonkit)
description: In Kiruna it is very common to get a glimpse of one of the two mountains which have taken shape as a result of the local mine, one to the south and one to the north. On the side of both mountains, different layers in the shape of a staircase may be seen, which is a very strong indication of the town. The mountains may also be spotted from the E10 west of the town.

title: Sweden - Gällivare Mountain (Plonkit)
description: In the town of Gällivare you can often see a mountain with a smooth slope and a low tree line to the southwest. No other town in Sweden has a natural treeless mountain in such close proximity.

title: Sweden - Omberg Landscape (Plonkit)
description: If you are surrounded by flat agricultural fields, with a single forested hill range to the west, you are likely to be east of Omberg in western Östergötland.

title: Sweden - Mälaren Mistletoe (Plonkit)
description: Mistletoe is mainly found near lake Mälaren and is particularly common in the city of Västerås.

title: Sweden - Visingsö Landscape (Plonkit)
description: The island of Visingsö in the middle of Lake Vättern can often be recognised by the agricultural fields with the lake being visible both to the northwest and southeast, with forested hills at the shore of either side of the lake.

title: Sweden - Orchards (Plonkit)
description:
A majority of all large orchards in Sweden are found around the town of Kivik on the east coast of Skåne.
Large orchards can also be found northeast of Kristianstad in Vånga, around Båstad, and on the southern east coast of lake Vättern.

title: Sweden - Öland Coast Road (Plonkit)
description: Following the northern west coast of Öland you will find this small coastal road, with a rocky beach and low, bushy vegetation.

title: Sweden - Fårö Landscape (Plonkit)
description: If you suspect you are on Gotland, and see small, dry stony fields with small juniper bushes, you are very likely to be on Fårö. This landscape becomes more extreme near the north coast of the island.

title: Sweden - Gotland South Tip (Plonkit)
description: On the southern tip of Gotland you can find this west coastal road with grassy fields and a grassy hill ridge to the east.

title: Sweden - Walloon Mills (Plonkit)
description: Near the coast north and east of Uppsala, you can come across old factory towns called Walloon mills. They typically consist of long rows of identical residential houses, which can either be made of brightly coloured stone or red wood, as well as small belfries, mansions and factory buildings, which are typically made in similar styles as the residential buildings.

title: Sweden - Slag Stone Buildings (Plonkit)
description: Buildings made fully or partially out of blue or green slag stone can occasionally be found in the mining region of Bergslagen.

title: Sweden - Öland Windmills (Plonkit)
description: Numerous small grey, and sometimes red, wooden windmills are spread across Öland. The island has more windmills than any other region in the country.

title: Sweden - Dalarna Chimneys (Plonkit)
description: Red brick chimneys with either a crown-like top or wide rectangular holes can be found close to lake Siljan in Dalarna county. It is somewhat common for these chimneys to be painted white.

title: Sweden - Visby Old Town (Plonkit)
description: Visby is the only preserved Hanseatic town in Sweden. The inner town can typically be recognised by the cobblestone streets, combined with the small, brightly painted stone houses and an abundance of roses following the house walls. It is also quite common to get a glimpse of the old Hanseatic wall surrounding the town.

title: Sweden - Stockholm Old Town (Plonkit)
description: The old town of Stockholm can be recognised by the old stone buildings, usually painted in warm colours, towering over the narrow cobblestone alleyways.

title: Sweden - Bus Stop Designs (Plonkit)
description:
Many cities and towns have their own local bus stop signs, which are different from the signs in the rest of the region (as shown in the infographic in section 2).
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Sweden - Neon School Bus Signs (Plonkit)
description: Neon-yellow school bus stop signs are commonly found in the municipalities of Linköping, Norrköping and Jönköping.

title: Sweden - Kungsbacka Bus Stops (Plonkit)
description: If you see Västra Götaland bus stops combined with three blue stripes as shown in the picture, you are in Kungsbacka municipality.

title: Sweden - Trams (Plonkit)
description: Trams can be found mostly in Gothenburg, secondly in Norrköping and Stockholm, and rarely on Generation 4 coverage in Lund.

title: Sweden - Västerås/Umeå Shelters (Plonkit)
description: Black bus shelters with this specific design, mainly recognised by the square ridge along the back of the roof, can be found in Västerås and Umeå.

title: Sweden - Stockholm Signs (Plonkit)
description: Street signs in Stockholm will have two rows divided by a black line and will usually lack a black border. Similar signs can also rarely be found in central Gävle.

title: Sweden - Gothenburg Signs (Plonkit)
description: The entire city of Gothenburg uses these unique blue street signs. Note that they almost always have two lines.

title: Sweden - Malmö Signs (Plonkit)
description: These somewhat old-looking, white street signs, with black corners, can be found all throughout Malmö.

title: Sweden - Ystad Signs (Plonkit)
description: Signs similar to the ones in Malmö, but with a yellow background can be found in Ystad.

title: Sweden - Vellinge Signs (Plonkit)
description: Blue street signs similar to the ones found in Gothenburg can be found in Vellinge municipality. Note that these normally only have one line, compared to the two lines on Gothenburg street signs.

title: Sweden - Falköping Signs (Plonkit)
description: Plain, yellow street signs can be found in Falköping. Note that yellow street signs may very rarely be seen in other towns, however they will always have a distinctly brighter colour.

title: Sweden - Köping Signs (Plonkit)
description: Blue street signs with a thin, black outline can be found in Köping.

title: Sweden - Siljan Street Names (Plonkit)
description: Street names ending in gattu or gatu are found in central Dalarna, near lake Siljan. Notably, gattu is found in the south of this area, while gatu is found in the north.

title: Sweden - Elfdalian Signs (Plonkit)
description: Elfdalian is a language that is exclusively found in and around Älvdalen. It is most commonly seen on street signs, with street names typically ending in “-ween” or “-weg”.

title: Sweden - Karlstad Stripes (Plonkit)
description: Three yellow stripes can be found on signposts and street lamps in Karlstad as well as on traffic lights in Stockholm.

title: Sweden - Tree Felling Signs (Plonkit)
description: These small yellow signs advertising tree felling are commonly found on utility poles and lamp posts in the suburbs of Stockholm. While the phone code for Stockholm is usually written on the signs, it is often difficult to make out from a distance.

title: Sweden - Sundsvall Dragons (Plonkit)
description: Sundsvall is known as Drakstaden (the Dragon City) in Sweden, which can be seen referenced in the form of dragon statues in the central parts of the city, and on signs.

title: Sweden - Birch Forests (Plonkit)
description: The stretch of the E4 between Umeå and the Finnish border is one of very few roads in the northern parts of the country which is large enough to normally have either a wide ditch or a barrier between the carriageways. The area is fairly flat and the road is mainly surrounded by forests, mostly consisting of thin birches and pines, which get lower further north.

title: Sweden - Snow-Capped Mountains (Plonkit)
description: If you are in a mountainous area with orange snow poles that have two wide reflectors close together, you are very likely to be near the Norwegian border on, or close to road E12.

title: Sweden - Gen 2 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: The stretch of road 95 closest to the Norwegian border can be recognized by a large number of yellow snow poles, all having two white reflectors. The coverage can be either Generation 2 in autumn or winter, or snowy Generation 4.

title: Sweden - Snow-Capped Mountains (Plonkit)
description: If you see a mixture of orange and yellow snow poles in a mountainous area, you should be on road E10 close to the Norwegian border.

title: Sweden - Snow-Capped Mountains (Plonkit)
description: Road 95 west of Arjeplog can be recognised by the Generation 4 thawing snow coverage in a mountainous landscape. The amount of snow significantly decreases as you go further east.

title: Sweden - Snow Coverage (Plonkit)
description: The city of Umeå has a lot of Generation 4 spring coverage, with dirty piles of thawing snow along almost every road. Almost no other city in the country has similar coverage.

title: Sweden - Birch Forests (Plonkit)
description: The stretch of the E45 going between Orsa and Älvros can be recognised by the brown-red wet pavement with forest consisting of thin pines and birches along the roadside.

title: Sweden - Gen 3 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: The island of Holmön has Generation 3 coverage, made by a white car with a long antenna, that features a distinctive visual glitch.

title: Sweden - Roof Smudge Meta (Plonkit)
description: Foskrosvägen, on the border between Jämtland and Dalarna, can be recognised by the slightly red dirt on the road, combined with several water smudges on the camera. A good way to find the road when scanning is to look for the “Reindeer spot point” right on the county border.

title: Sweden - Swedish Language (Plonkit)
description: Swedish is a North Germanic language that is closely related to Danish and Norwegian. The Swedish alphabet contains the special letters Å, Ä and Ö.

title: Sweden - Southern Beech Forests (Plonkit)
description: Beech forests, which can generally be recognised by the barren ground covered in brown leafs, are mainly found in the far south.

title: Sweden - Regional Bus Shelters (Plonkit)
description: Many regions have their own distinct type of bus shelters, which may either replace or complement the bus stop signs. This image contains the ones which are most common and easily recognizable.

title: Sweden - Area Codes (Plonkit)
description: The first 3-4 (2 in Stockholm) digits of landline phone numbers in Sweden are the area code. The map shows the first two digits in every region. Within the regions, the third and fourth digit of area codes typically increase to the northeast.

title: Sweden - Local Bus Signs (Plonkit)
description: Many cities and towns have their own local bus stop signs, which are different from the signs in the rest of the region (as shown in the infographic in section 2).

title: Switzerland - Low-Cam Coverage (Plonkit)
description:
By far the most important way to recognize Switzerland, is that all car coverage is low-cam. This means that the camera on the Google car is intentionally set up lower than in most other countries. This can be recognized in two ways:
- The car blur is significantly bigger.
- Roads look wider and objects around you are seen from a lower angle.
Generally, the bigger car blur is the most consistent way to recognize low-cam.

title: Switzerland - Swiss Plates (Plonkit)
description:
Swiss licence plates differ substantially from other European plates. They are fully white and lack the blue strip found in most other European countries.
Front plates are extremely short compared to most in Europe.
Rear plates can be either long or tall. In both cases the red country emblem can be seen on the left, while the canton emblem can be seen on the right.

title: Switzerland - Swiss Bollards (Plonkit)
description: Swiss bollards are black-and-white with white or grey reflectors. They can be either wedge-shaped or cylindrical with a rounded top.

title: Switzerland - Directional Sign Colors (Plonkit)
description:
The colour of directional signs indicates which type of road you are on. Main road signs will be blue, while side roads are white.
Major place names will frequently appear on blue signs, while smaller places tend to be on white signs. However, you can still find large city names on a white sign.

title: Switzerland - Pedestrian Signs (Plonkit)
description: Swiss pedestrian signs have seven stripes, making it almost unique for Europe. Furthermore, rather than the typical European square shape, the signs appear as tall blue rectangles.

title: Switzerland - Yellow Road Lines (Plonkit)
description: Long dashed yellow road lines are a good clue for Switzerland.

title: Switzerland - Yellow Crosswalks (Plonkit)
description: Pedestrian crossings are typically painted yellow and exclusive to Switzerland and Liechtenstein within Europe.

title: Switzerland - Sign Metal Borders (Plonkit)
description: Swiss road signs commonly have a round, grey metal border around them.

title: Switzerland - Town Entry Signs (Plonkit)
description: Town entry signs in Switzerland are usually white or blue, with a metal frame around them.

title: Switzerland - Swiss Chevrons (Plonkit)
description: Chevrons are black with a white arrow. You may also rarely find chevrons that are white with a black arrow.

title: Switzerland - Landscape Overview (Plonkit)
description: While the southern half of Switzerland is extremely mountainous, with long, thin valleys between the mountains, the northern half mostly consists of large farmlands on either flat ground or rolling hills, typically with forested hills in the distance.

title: Switzerland - Swiss Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Swiss and Alpine architecture in general largely consists of stone buildings painted in light and warm colours, often combined with wooden parts and details. Roofs are typically tiled and of a gable type. It is extremely common for windows to have wooden shutters which open horizontally in two parts.

title: Switzerland - Bus Stop Frames (Plonkit)
description: These bus stop signs, with thick metal signposts going around them, are unique to Switzerland.

title: Switzerland - Official Languages (Plonkit)
description: Switzerland has four official languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh, which are spoken in the regions shown. Note that some areas, mostly near the region borders, are bilingual.

title: Switzerland - Speed Limit Languages (Plonkit)
description: The text on the speed limit signs varies depending on the official languages in the region.

title: Switzerland - Canton Abbreviations (Plonkit)
description: Cantons are the first-level administrative division of Switzerland. It is very common to find the two-letter abbreviation for the canton that you are in, as seen on some town entry signs. As such, remembering these can be a great asset when region-guessing Switzerland.

title: Switzerland - Postal Codes (Plonkit)
description: The first digits of Swiss postal codes are a good way to regionguess the country. The general pattern is that the numbers increase from the west to east.

title: Switzerland - Elevation Map (Plonkit)
description: Elevation is an important part of region-guessing Switzerland. The southern half of Switzerland is extremely mountainous, while the northern half mostly has smaller mountains and hills.

title: Switzerland - Northwest Hills (Plonkit)
description: A fairly flat landscape with a long chain of medium-sized, forested mountains northwest means you are likely south of the Jura Mountains.

title: Switzerland - Jura Limestone (Plonkit)
description: Exposed limestone rocks, protruding from forested hills, are commonly found in the Jura mountains.

title: Switzerland - Rock Walls (Plonkit)
description: Rock walls are mainly found in the Jura mountains, but can also be found in the Alps, particularly in the Italian speaking parts.

title: Switzerland - Ticino Architecture (Plonkit)
description:
Not unexpectedly, seeing typical Italian architecture in Switzerland should imply that you are in the Italian-speaking areas in the south, principally the canton of Ticino.
The architectural style is characterized by, typically very smooth, orange-yellow stone walls with multiple floors and orange or brownish tiled roofs. Green and brown Italian-style window shutters are common.

title: Switzerland - Bern Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Large houses with thick roofs, which are shaped like an arch underneath, are common around Bern.

title: Switzerland - Northeast Timber Frames (Plonkit)
description: Elaborate timber frames, which are commonly painted red, are found in the northeast.

title: Switzerland - Appenzell Architecture (Plonkit)
description:
Around Appenzell, most houses will consist of a large living house connected to a long barn, such that the roof of the living house and the barn are at a 90° angle.
The front facade of the living house will often be divided into small squares, with each window being perfectly contained within a square.

title: Switzerland - Canton Graubünden (Plonkit)
description: In the canton of Graubünden, you will often come across houses entirely made of stone, with, most commonly white, decorative painted details around windows and the edges of the house.

title: Switzerland - Vaud Town Signs (Plonkit)
description: These large town entry signs can sometimes be found in the canton of Vaud.

title: Switzerland - Basel-Landschaft Green (Plonkit)
description: Olive green infrastructure, particularly signposts, sign borders and sign backs, are found in Basel-Landschaft.

title: Switzerland - Valais Wooden Bollards (Plonkit)
description: In the canton of Valais, you will often see thick wooden bollards, which can either be square-shaped or cylindrical.

title: Switzerland - Glarus Fence Reflectors (Plonkit)
description: In place of bollards, reflectors in the canton of Glarus will often be attached to fences following the road.

title: Switzerland - Geneva Bike Symbols (Plonkit)
description: In Geneva and in the valley between Martigny and Lake Geneva, you can find bike path symbols painted on the road with a simplified person on top of two disconnected wheels.

title: Switzerland - Road Divider Map (Plonkit)
description:
You may find several different types of road dividers across the country, distributed as seen in this graphic.
This image was provided by quarksauce. You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Switzerland - Lake Geneva Hills (Plonkit)
description: If the area around your location appears hilly, but not mountainous, and you manage to catch a glimpse of a large lake to the south, with tall mountains on the other side, then you are very likely north of Lake Geneva.

title: Switzerland - Lake Constance (Plonkit)
description: Seeing a wide lake to the northeast, situated in a landscape with relatively low elevation, means you should be looking at Lake Constance (on some Maps labelled as the Bodensee).

title: Switzerland - Martigny Fruit Trees (Plonkit)
description: The valley of Martigny has the highest density of fruit plantations in the country. It can easily be recognized by the many small fruit trees in combination with the wide, flat valley with large mountains on either side.

title: Switzerland - Fruit Tree Distribution (Plonkit)
description: Apart from the valley of Martigny, the most likely area to find fruit trees is near Lake Constance, followed by the area northwest of Lake Geneva.

title: Switzerland - Canton Graubünden (Plonkit)
description: In the canton of Graubünden, you can find this unique and easily recognizable train coverage on the tracks of the “Bernina Express.” It runs around most of the canton, all the way down to Tirano in Italy.

title: Switzerland - Gen 2 Locations (Plonkit)
description: Generation 2 coverage is very limited in Switzerland. It can be found mostly near the border between the cantons of Bern and Valais, and on a few very short stretches in Schaffhausen.

title: Switzerland - St. Gallen Signs (Plonkit)
description: These blue street signs, with rounded edges on the sides, are unique to the city of Sankt Gallen.

title: Switzerland - Basel Signs (Plonkit)
description: Large blue street signs, attached to a low double signpost, similar to directional signs in Denmark, are found in Basel.

title: Switzerland - Bern Old Town (Plonkit)
description: Downtown Bern can be recognized by this specific architecture. Grey toned buildings, typically with four floors and large, somewhat rounded openings lined up on the ground floor are common.

title: Ukraine - Ukrainian Plates (Plonkit)
description:
Ukraine uses long, white licence plates, with a distinctive blue and yellow strip on the left (the colours of the flag).
You may also come across older plates, where the blue and yellow are difficult to spot.

title: Ukraine - Gen 2 Coverage (Plonkit)
description:
All coverage in Ukraine is Generation 3. Most of it was made using a red Google car. This car is almost unique to Ukraine. It sometimes has an antenna, and sometimes no antenna. Note that the car is not always visible, though at times you will still be able to tell its colour due to the car blur glitch.
- Most importantly, you will not find the red Generation 3 car in Russia.
- Russia can have Generation 4 (and sometimes Generation 2). Ukraine never has either Generation.
- Russian Generation 3 cars always have either a short or long antenna. If you see no antenna at all, consider Ukraine.
Also note that some parts of Belgium can have a red google car with a long antenna.

title: Ukraine - Other Google Cars (Plonkit)
description:
More rarely, you can also find several other Google cars in Ukraine:
- Black car with a long antenna
- White car with a long antenna
- Grey car with a short antenna
These cars can be found in multiple countries, including Russia. See the region guessing section to see where you can find these cars within Ukraine.

title: Ukraine - Poor Road Quality (Plonkit)
description:
On average, Ukraine has some of the worst roads in Europe. Most rural roads have lots of potholes, cracks and warped pavement.
This abysmal road quality can really help with tough 50-50s with Russia, which generally has somewhat better roads.

title: Ukraine - Patriotic Streetside (Plonkit)
description: Many random streetside objects are painted in the colours of the Ukrainian flag: blue and yellow. Most commonly, you will see fences that have this colour.

title: Ukraine - Unique Letters (Plonkit)
description:
The Ukrainian language uses the Cyrillic script.
These letters are unique to Ukrainian, compared to Russian:
- Є є (not to be confused with Э э in Russian and Belarusian.)
- Ґ ґ
- І і
- Ї ї

title: Ukraine - Word for Street (Plonkit)
description:
The Ukrainian word for street is вулиця (vulytsya), abbreviated вул. (vul.).
The Russian word is улица, abbreviated ул., without a в at the beginning.

title: Ukraine - Word for City (Plonkit)
description: The Ukrainian word for city is місто (misto), abbreviated м. (m.). It can be used both to differentiate it from other Cyrillic languages and to quickly find the city name in addresses.

title: Ukraine - Painted Square Poles (Plonkit)
description:
Ukraine primarily uses square concrete poles. They can have a variety of different pole tops, and sometimes have white paint at the bottom.
These poles are similar to the ones found in other post-Soviet countries like Russia and Lithuania.

title: Ukraine - Diagonal Support Poles (Plonkit)
description: Poles often have diagonal support beams.

title: Ukraine - Wooden Support Poles (Plonkit)
description: You can also find wooden poles, sometimes with concrete support blocks at their base.

title: Ukraine - Red Chevrons (Plonkit)
description:
Ukraine uses a red chevron with white arrows.
Russia and Estonia use the same chevrons.

title: Ukraine - Pedestrian Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Ukrainian pedestrian signs have three stripes.
Russia, Estonia and Lithuania also use pedestrian signs with three stripes.

title: Ukraine - Town Entry Signs (Plonkit)
description: Ukraine uses white town entry signs.

title: Ukraine - BW Guardrails (Plonkit)
description: Guardrails and barriers will often be painted black and white, similar to Russia.

title: Ukraine - Soviet Apartments (Plonkit)
description:
In bigger cities and towns, you will often see big Soviet-era apartment blocks. These are often made of light grey brick. They tend to look fairly rundown and poorly maintained. Some are made of concrete prefab units that are stacked on top of each other.
These apartment buildings are similar to those found in Russian cities. You can also find this style of building in the Baltic countries, but these tend to look better maintained.

title: Ukraine - Suburban Homes (Plonkit)
description: Single-family homes are very common in suburbs and small towns. These neighbourhoods are often heavily vegetated and tend to look rundown. Most roads are unpaved. Buildings are usually made of bricks, often have corrugated roofs, and are invariably surrounded by fences.

title: Ukraine - Rural Landscape (Plonkit)
description:
This is the stereotypical rural round in Ukraine:
- Generally bad road quality.
- A landscape that is usually flat or slightly hilly.
- A line of trees or bushes next to the road, with wide open agricultural fields beyond that.
- A lack of road infrastructure or buildings, until you reach the next urban area.
- Low amount of traffic.

title: Ukraine - Summer Coverage (Plonkit)
description:
Almost all Ukrainian coverage was made in the summer, meaning the foliage is green and the people around are dressed for sunny weather.
Five major cities have autumn coverage, with distinct fall colours and colder weather. See the region guessing section for more information.

title: Ukraine - Poplar Trees (Plonkit)
description: These tall poplar trees are common in many parts of the country.

title: Ukraine - Coverage Distribution (Plonkit)
description:
Coverage in Ukraine is mostly limited to urban areas and the main roads between them. See the region-guessing section for a map.
However, one type of coverage that can sometimes trick people are ultra-rural tracks close to cities. This is a decently common type of coverage in Ukraine, despite the general rule that most coverage is either urban or on a main road.

title: Ukraine - Coverage Map (Plonkit)
description:
This is a map of street view coverage in Ukraine. Most coverage between cities is on yellow roads.
Notably, there is almost no coverage in the southeast. The only exception is Donetsk. There is also no coverage south of Odesa in the area near Romania.
You can view the extent of official coverage on this site.

title: Ukraine - Area Codes (Plonkit)
description:
Ukrainian landline phone numbers start with a two-digit area code. Each oblast has its own area code. If the third digit is a 2, it refers to a phone number in the oblast’s capital (typically the biggest city).
Mobile phone numbers start with 50, 63, 66-68, 73 or 91-99. They are not unique to a geographic area.

title: Ukraine - Plate Codes (Plonkit)
description: The first two letters on Ukrainian licence plates determine in which oblast the vehicle is registered in, making unblurred licence plates very useful for regionguessing. Unlike most regional plates in Europe, they’re not intuitive, so learning the codes beforehand is essential for utilising them.

title: Ukraine - Internet Domains (Plonkit)
description: Oblast-specific second-level internet domains can occasionally be found in Ukraine. Seen in the image is the domain for Ternopil Oblast (.te.ua). They can typically be used without being memorised, as they’re mostly intuitive. You can however learn them here.

title: Ukraine - Ukraine Features (Plonkit)
description: May coverage in Ukraine is primarily seen in the western half of the country. It can be recognized by looking at the plants, which have a yellowish tint on otherwise green leaves.

title: Ukraine - 2011 Fall Coverage (Plonkit)
description:
Five major cities were covered in 2011, years before the rest of the country was covered: Kyiv, Lviv, Kharkiv, Odesa and Donetsk.
This coverage was made during autumn, meaning that the trees have distinct fall colours and people are dressed for colder weather.
In Kyiv, Lviv and Kharkiv, almost all of this coverage has been overwritten by the newer summer coverage. However, in all of Donetsk, and most of Odesa, it is still intact. In Donetsk specifically, there is no newer coverage at all.

title: Ukraine - 2011 Car Meta (Plonkit)
description:
This older 2011 coverage was made with a black or white Google car, instead of the standard red one. Both cars have a long antenna.
The black car was used in Donetsk. Note that Donetsk has no newer coverage whatsoever, so never guess in that city if you see a red car.
The white car was used in Lviv, Kyiv and Kharkiv. As the coverage in these cities is mostly overwritten, the white car is very rare.

title: Ukraine - Carpathian Forests (Plonkit)
description: The Carpathian Mountains is an area in western Ukraine that is significantly hillier than the rest of the country, in some places bordering on mountainous. It is also much more forested, with very little agriculture, and a lot of pine trees. The roads going through it tend to be more curvy, rather than the straight highways found in the rest of the country.

title: Ukraine - Northern Pine Forests (Plonkit)
description:
Forests with Baltic pines (Pinus sylvestris) are most commonly found in the north, most often near the border with Belarus. Baltic pines are usually tall and have orange-red bark.
While some of these forests consist solely of this species, many of them are a mix of Baltic pines and broadleaf trees.

title: Ukraine - Southern Climate (Plonkit)
description: Towards the south, the climate becomes warmer and drier. The landscape is more arid. Forests are considerably more rare, and make way for shrubs and open fields. The difference is not extreme, but can become noticeable after some practice.

title: Ukraine - Sunflower Fields (Plonkit)
description:
Sunflowers are grown in most of Ukraine. However, they only start to bloom as early as late July. Due to the way Ukraine was covered, this means you will usually only see sunflower fields that are in bloom in the far south and east of the country.
These fields are most common in Kherson, Mykolaiv and Odesa Oblast. The road T0403 to Nova Kakhovka especially has a lot of them.
Note that sunflower fields that are not in bloom can be found in most of the country. These will just look like regular crop fields to most people.

title: Ukraine - Russian Language (Plonkit)
description:
The Russian language can be found in Ukraine, particularly in the east and south. While there are several differences between Russian and Ukrainian, these are some of the most noteworthy:
- The letters Ы ы, Э э are only found in Russian.
- The Russian word for street is улица, abbreviated ул.
- The Russian word for city is город, abbreviated г.

title: Ukraine - Leaf Antenna Meta (Plonkit)
description: A leaf can be seen on the back of the Google car from: Ternopil to Zolochiv on the H02, Ternopil to Brody on the P39, and from Brody to Dubno on the E40. It can also be seen from Brody to Pochaiv on the P26 and from Dubno to Mlyniv on the E85.

title: Ukraine - Odesa Silver Car (Plonkit)
description: The older 2011 coverage in Odesa was made using a silver car with a short antenna, rather than a black or white car with a long antenna. The car may sometimes be fully blurred.

title: Ukraine - Kryvyi Rih Red Soil (Plonkit)
description: Red soil can be seen on some ultra-rural dirt tracks around the iron mine in Kryvyi Rih, due to mining activity. Brazilian-style poles can also be seen, making locations around the mine very convincing bait. The foliage, however, will be significantly less tropical, and a long antenna can be seen.

title: Ukraine - Kryvyi Rih Red Band (Plonkit)
description: These poles, with a red band across them, are unique to Kryvyi Rih.

title: Ukraine - Sunflower Bus Stops (Plonkit)
description: Bus stop shelters with a vibrant yellow-and-green paint scheme, featuring sunflowers and the name of a local brand (Оліс), can be found in the Mykolaiv and Kherson oblasts.

title: Ukraine - Ivano-Frankivsk Glitch (Plonkit)
description: Within Ukraine, this visual glitch is unique to the city of Ivano-Frankivsk.

title: Ukraine - Red-Reflector Bollards (Plonkit)
description:
These “Polish” bollards can be found in the Zakarpattia Oblast. They have a red reflector that wraps around the bollard.
They are identical to the standard bollard used in Poland (hence the name).

title: Ukraine - Hungarian Signs (Plonkit)
description: The area near the border with Hungary is majority Hungarian. As a result, you will see a lot of signs with Hungarian language on it – bilingual or even monolingual.

title: Ukraine - Hungarian Architecture (Plonkit)
description: In addition, the villages in this region look similar to Hungarian architecture. Settlements are fairly linear and organised, with predominantly single-storey houses that are closer to the street. Many roofs have orange tiles or diamond-shaped slate tiles that are similar to roofs found in central European countries like Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia.

title: Ukraine - Chernobyl Coverage (Plonkit)
description:
Google sent a special car trekker to the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone, where the nuclear disaster happened in the 1980s. This car goes from Ivankiv all the way to the abandoned town of Pripyat.
On most of the road to Pripyat, you will not really be able to tell that you are inside the Exclusion Zone. However, inside Pripyat you will see completely abandoned and overgrown buildings, giving the place an eerie look.

title: Ukraine - Chernobyl Yellow Flag (Plonkit)
description: On one side of the road going to Chernobyl, a yellow flag with an Opel logo can be seen on the Google car’s antenna.

title: Ukraine - Red Car Meta (Plonkit)
description: All coverage in Ukraine is Generation 3. Most of it was made using a red Google car. This car is almost unique to Ukraine. It sometimes has an antenna, and sometimes no antenna. Note that the car is not always visible, though at times you will still be able to tell its colour due to the car blur glitch.

title: United Kingdom - UK Plates (Plonkit)
description:
UK front plates are white, while back plates are yellow. Some plates have a blue strip on the left, but most do not.
Additionally, you might see a plate with a green ‘Zero Emissions’ strip.

title: United Kingdom - Left-Hand Traffic (Plonkit)
description: The UK drives on the left side of the road.

title: United Kingdom - No Stopping Lines (Plonkit)
description: Double yellow road lines are often found on the sides of marked roads, especially in urban areas. These lines indicate a no stopping zone.

title: United Kingdom - UK Middle Lines (Plonkit)
description: These middle lines, that consist of long dashes with cat’s eyes (reflectors) in the gaps between the dashes, are a good clue for the UK.

title: United Kingdom - UK Bollards (Plonkit)
description: The most common bollard in the UK looks like this. It has a rounded shape, with a red reflector on the front and a white one on the back. The base and top are black, with a white stripe in the middle.

title: United Kingdom - Pole Steps (Plonkit)
description: The UK uses wooden poles. Pole steps bolted on the side of the pole are very common. These pole steps are shaped like a series of thin horizontal metal rods.

title: United Kingdom - Metal Poles (Plonkit)
description: Poles in the UK occasionally have a metal crossbar near the top with two diagonal supports forming a triangle shape.

title: United Kingdom - Black-White Chevrons (Plonkit)
description: Chevrons are black with white arrows.

title: United Kingdom - Warning Signs (Plonkit)
description: Like most European countries, the UK uses triangular warning signs with a red border and a white background.

title: United Kingdom - Directional Signs (Plonkit)
description: Direction signs in the United Kingdom can be blue, green, or white. Look for the letters A or M, as these are the major roads in the country. Smaller roads start with B.

title: United Kingdom - Street Signs (Plonkit)
description:
The UK commonly uses these white street signs with black text, that are positioned low to the ground. They are usually supported by two small posts. Many street signs in suburban areas will have a small cul-de-sac icon.
They can sometimes have different colours or feature small designs, like coats of arms.

title: United Kingdom - Give Way Sign (Plonkit)
description: UK yield signs feature the phrase “GIVE WAY”.

title: United Kingdom - Danger of Death (Plonkit)
description:
The yellow warning stickers on utility poles can be a good way to distinguish between the UK and Ireland.
The most important difference is that UK stickers feature a guy getting zapped by a lightning bolt.
The Irish stickers usually have a lightning bolt, but lack the guy getting zapped. They also often have an extra second rectangular sticker with a black outline, below the lightning bolt.

title: United Kingdom - Yellow Bollards (Plonkit)
description: This yellow traffic bollard is commonly found in the UK.

title: United Kingdom - Belisha Beacons (Plonkit)
description: Pedestrian crossing signs are almost non-existent in the UK. Instead, pedestrian crossings will often have these distinctive black and white striped poles, with a yellow light bulb on top.

title: United Kingdom - Square Metal Gates (Plonkit)
description: Rural metal gates with square corners are very common in the UK.

title: United Kingdom - British Countryside (Plonkit)
description: The British countryside tends to be very green, with lots of hedgerows lining the road. Low, rolling hills are common throughout most of the country.

title: United Kingdom - Terraced Houses (Plonkit)
description: Terraced houses (row houses) are very common in the UK. This housing type shares walls on both sides with neighbouring homes. You will also see a lot of semi-detached houses, which share just one side wall with another house.

title: United Kingdom - Red Brick Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Red brick buildings are common in many parts of the UK.

title: United Kingdom - Suburban Estates (Plonkit)
description: Suburbs in UK towns tend to have a recognizable look. They typically feature near-identical houses, often semi-detached, usually with well-manicured lawns. The road layout can be maze-like, with lots of cul-de-sacs and curvy roads.

title: United Kingdom - Chimney Pots (Plonkit)
description: Many British buildings have distinct-looking chimneys with multiple so-called chimney pots. These pots are usually round and brick-coloured.

title: United Kingdom - Timber Framing (Plonkit)
description: Some buildings, both old and new, feature black-and-white timber framing.

title: United Kingdom - Smallcam Meta (Plonkit)
description: The UK has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.

title: United Kingdom - Country Flags (Plonkit)
description: Occasionally, you can find one of the 4 country flags, which will tell you where in the UK you are.

title: United Kingdom - Road Numbers (Plonkit)
description:
A- and B-roads are grouped by their first digit, for example A380 and B3217 are located in the southwest of the country. Motorways also generally follow this pattern.
Beware that roads starting with any digit from 1 to 8 can also be found in Northern Ireland.

title: United Kingdom - Phone Area Codes (Plonkit)
description:
Landline phone numbers in the UK always have nine or ten digits after the 0 trunk code. The first two to four digits after the 0 are the area code. Unfortunately for Geoguessr players, there is not much rhyme or reason to their geographic ordering.
However, the area codes of some large cities are still worth memorising. The most important ones are summarised in this infographic. Notably, all of Northern Ireland uses the phone code 028, and all of London uses 020.
A complete overview of all other area codes is available in this infographic.

title: United Kingdom - City Bins (Plonkit)
description: Bins in urban areas often have the city name on them.

title: United Kingdom - Mountain Terrain (Plonkit)
description:
The Scottish Highlands can be distinguished by the semi-barren, very mountainous landscape.
In addition, some of the most mountainous parts of Wales and Northern England can look similar.

title: United Kingdom - Scottish Bollards (Plonkit)
description:
In Scotland, you can often find these red and white bollards. They are round, bulky, and have a red-and-grey reflector that wraps all the way around.
They are sometimes found in other parts of the UK.

title: United Kingdom - Passing Places (Plonkit)
description: These diamond-shaped ‘Passing Place’ signs are most commonly found in Scotland.

title: United Kingdom - Welsh Language (Plonkit)
description:
Welsh is a Celtic language that is spoken throughout Wales. Road signs in Wales are usually bilingual English and Welsh. Towns often have Welsh names too.
Welsh uses the letters D, W, and Y much more commonly than English. The double LL is also very distinct.

title: United Kingdom - Bilingual Markings (Plonkit)
description: In Wales, markings on the road are in both English and Welsh. One of the best examples of this is ‘Araf’, which means ‘Slow’. This marking is only found in Wales.

title: United Kingdom - Gaelic Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Scottish Gaelic is a Celtic language that is closely related to Irish. They have a very similar look and use accent marks commonly. Common and recognizable letter clusters include bh, dh, fh, mh, ai, ea, eo, and ui.
Scottish Gaelic on road signs is found most commonly in the Scottish Highlands, and is almost always found north of Glasgow.

title: United Kingdom - Scottish Stone Architecture (Plonkit)
description: It is common to see houses made of large blocks of sandstone or granite in Scotland. Granite buildings are common in Aberdeen, red sandstone is common in Glasgow and Dumfries, and yellow sandstone is common in Edinburgh.

title: United Kingdom - Cornish Palms (Plonkit)
description: Cornish palms (Cordyline australis) in the UK are most commonly found in the far southwest along the coast and in Jersey. Although, they can rarely be found all along the west coast up to Scotland.

title: United Kingdom - Northern Ireland Stickers (Plonkit)
description: These black stickers with yellow text sometimes appear on lampposts in Northern Ireland.

title: United Kingdom - Utility Poles (Plonkit)
description: Warning stickers wrapped all the way around the utility pole are specific to Northern Ireland.

title: United Kingdom - Isle of Man Gen 2 (Plonkit)
description:
The Isle of Man is an island in the Irish Sea between the United Kingdom and Ireland. There is only Generation 2 coverage on the island. For country streak purposes, it is counted as part of the United Kingdom.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to the Isle of Man here.

title: United Kingdom - Jersey Gen 2 (Plonkit)
description:
Jersey is an island in the English Channel between France and England. There is only Generation 2 coverage on the island. For country streak purposes, it is counted as part of the United Kingdom.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Jersey here.

title: United Kingdom - Gibraltar (Plonkit)
description:
Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory located at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, bordering Spain. For country streak purposes, the territory is counted as part of the United Kingdom.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Gibraltar here.

title: United Kingdom - Bermuda (Plonkit)
description:
Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory located in the North Atlantic Ocean.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Bermuda here.

title: United Kingdom - Falkland Islands (Plonkit)
description:
The Falkland Islands is a British Overseas Territory located in the South Atlantic Ocean.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to the Falkland Islands here.

title: United Kingdom - South Georgia (Plonkit)
description:
South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands is a British Overseas Territory located in the South Atlantic Ocean.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to the territory here.

title: United Kingdom - Pitcairn Islands (Plonkit)
description:
The Pitcairn Islands is a British Overseas Territory located in the South Pacific Ocean.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to the Pitcairn Islands here.

title: United Kingdom - British Indian Ocean Territory (Plonkit)
description:
The British Indian Ocean Territory is a British Overseas Territory, unsurprisingly located in the Indian Ocean.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to the British Indian Ocean Territory here.

title: United Kingdom - The Lake District (Plonkit)
description: The Lake District is very hilly, with a lot of exposed rocks and stone walls. It can look like the Scottish Highlands, but Scotland is generally less rocky.

title: United Kingdom - London Street Signs (Plonkit)
description: London street signs have a distinct look. They usually feature the street name in black, followed by the postcode and borough in red.

title: United Kingdom - Aberdeen Signs (Plonkit)
description: Street name signs in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire typically feature a simple blue background with white lettering.

title: United Kingdom - Townland Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Signs with green text underneath the street name, indicating the townland, can be found in the western part of Northern Ireland.
Especially towards the north of the shaded area, there may be a metal divider between the two lines.

title: United Kingdom - White Street Signs (Plonkit)
description: Most street signs in the Wakefield council are black with a white outline and letters. They use the Monotype Rockwell Nova font.

title: United Kingdom - London Electric Car (Plonkit)
description: Some of the Generation 4 coverage in London was taken by a white electric vehicle, with this distinct back of the car visible.

title: United Kingdom - Birmingham Yellow Tape (Plonkit)
description: The majority of poles and signposts in Birmingham have either yellow tape or yellow paint wrapped around them. Lampposts will also usually have this yellow sticker.

title: United Kingdom - Twenty's Plenty (Plonkit)
description: Speed signs with green borders with the text “Twenty’s Plenty” are mostly found in and around Glasgow.

title: United Kingdom - Scottish Highlands (Plonkit)
description: The Scottish Highlands can be distinguished by the semi-barren, very mountainous landscape.

title: Alaska - Yellow Plates (Plonkit)
description: The most common and recognisable Alaskan licence plate is all yellow. In Generation 4 coverage you can also get a plate with a large orange circle in the middle. Front plates are required in Alaska.

title: Alaska - Alaskan Highway Shield (Plonkit)
description: The Alaskan highway shield has an image of the Big Dipper constellation on the bottom left.

title: Alaska - Alaska Features (Plonkit)
description: Trees in Alaska are generally thinner and have less broad leaves than those seen in the other 49 states.

title: Alaska - Snow-Capped Mountains (Plonkit)
description: On a lot of the Alaskan coverage you will be able to see tall, snow covered mountains.

title: Alaska - Gen 2 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: In most of the US, Generation 2 is rare. However, Alaska has a fair amount of Generation 2 coverage.

title: Alaska - Alaska Has Generation (Plonkit)
description: Alaska has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front, with the front of the white car being very visible. The blur can also be fully transparent.

title: Alaska - Shitcam Coverage (Plonkit)
description: Alaska is the only state in the US where shitcam coverage is prevalent. This coverage is lower resolution with more faded colours, compared to other camera generations. Also, a large blur can be seen at the bottom of the page.

title: Alaska - Alaska Features (Plonkit)
description: Generation 4 coverage in Alaska is concentrated around the city of Anchorage.

title: Alaska - Most Interior And (Plonkit)
description: Most of interior and northern Alaska lies in subarctic or tundra climate zones. These areas feature relatively low amounts of forest undergrowth and shorter trees.

title: Alaska - Gen 2 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: The Alaskan towns in the Alexander Archipelago, on the British Columbia border have a unique look. Tall mountains with lush green forests can be seen in the background, with the majority of buildings made of wood. In addition, Generation 2 coverage is often overcast and misty.

title: Alaska - Alaska Features (Plonkit)
description: The only two major urban areas in Alaska are Anchorage and Fairbanks.

title: Alaska - Mountain Terrain (Plonkit)
description: Most of the suburban areas in Alaska are in and around Anchorage.These areas feature wide roads, commercial districts, and sometimes heavy traffic. Mountains can commonly be seen in the distance.

title: Alaska - Aspen Trees Populus (Plonkit)
description: Aspen trees (Populus tremuloides) can be found in lower elevation areas of interior and south-central regions of Alaska. These trees have white bark and rounded leaves.

title: Alaska - Valley Landscape (Plonkit)
description: Due to Alaska’s very cold climate; agricultural fields are mainly found in the south of the state, mostly in the Matanuska Valley and Kenai Peninsula.

title: Alaska - Alaskan Pipeline Which (Plonkit)
description: The Alaskan pipeline which is usually visible from main roads, can be seen at these points. This is an easy way to identify Alaska as there are no similar pipelines in the rest of the US.

title: Alaska - Mountain Terrain (Plonkit)
description: Juneau, Alaska’s Capital city, is the largest settlement in the Alaskan panhandle. Therefore, it is much more ‘built up’ than other towns in this area. The city is surrounded by heavily forested mountains and hills.

title: Alaska - Anchorage Features (Plonkit)
description: Fire hydrants in Anchorage are typically pale pink or pale yellow in colour.

title: Alaska - Fairbanks Features (Plonkit)
description: Fire hydrants in Fairbanks are commonly either bright yellow or a combination of colours (most commonly yellow and blue).

title: Alaska - Shitcam Coverage (Plonkit)
description: Shitcam is only found around Anchorage and Fairbanks, and parts of the road that connects them.

title: Alaska - North End Dalton (Plonkit)
description: The North end of the Dalton Highway features a flat and snowy landscape and an overcast sky. A small ridge of hills can be seen to the west of the highway in certain spots.

title: Alaska - Gen 2 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: The Denali highway, stretching from Cantwell to Paxson in central Alaska, is a mostly gravel highway in the ‘Alaska’ mountain range. This road runs generally east to west, is covered in the generation 2 camera, and was taken in late summer, so wildflowers and green shrubby plants are common.

title: Alaska - Gen 2 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: The Steese Highway is another gravel highway that goes from Fairbanks to the town of ‘Central.’ Similar to the Denali highway, this road runs generally east to west and is covered in generation 2. The difference, however, is that the mountains along this road are noticeably lower than the ones adjacent to the Denali Highway.

title: Alaska - Gen 2 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: Highway 5, from the Yukon border to Tetlin Junction, can be recognized by the foggy, rainy weather, and Generation 2 camera.

title: Alaska - Prudhoe City (Plonkit)
description: Prudhoe Bay, the northernmost town in America covered by street view, can be recognized by cold, dead landscape, overcast clouds and lack of tall buildings. A second Google car can sometimes be seen.

title: Alaska - Nome Unalakleet And (Plonkit)
description: Nome, Unalakleet and Galena are three isolated Alaskan towns which are covered only by trekker. The trekker’s lime green hat or black and white beanie can be seen.

title: Alaska - Map Shows Which (Plonkit)
description: This map shows which parts of Alaska have coverage and which camera generation was used to cover each road.

title: Bermuda - Bermuda Location (Plonkit)
description: Bermuda is a British overseas territory, located north of the Caribbean sea. As such, it is counted as the United Kingdom for country streaks purposes.

title: Bermuda - Left-Hand Traffic (Plonkit)
description: Bermuda drives on the left side of the road.

title: Bermuda - Black Google Car (Plonkit)
description: Bermuda features a black Street View car with the entire front sides of the vehicle typically visible.

title: Bermuda - Vegetation & Houses (Plonkit)
description: The most typical look of Bermuda is somewhat dense vegetation, consisting of fairly small trees and a lot of bushes, combined with single family houses strewn across the landscape.

title: Bermuda - Bermuda Plates (Plonkit)
description: Bermudan licence plates are all-white, fairly long, and with black digits, somewhat contained to the middle of the plate.

title: Bermuda - Single Yellow Line (Plonkit)
description: Most roads in Bermuda contain a single solid yellow middle line with no outer road lines.

title: Bermuda - Zig-Zag Lines (Plonkit)
description: You will occasionally see these white zig zag road lines on Bermuda.

title: Bermuda - Pastel Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Most buildings on Bermuda are single family stone houses painted in pastel colours. They will almost always have completely white roofs.

title: Bermuda - Palms (Plonkit)
description: Palms are very commonly found on Bermuda.

title: Bermuda - Blue Water (Plonkit)
description: On Bermuda you will never be far away from the ocean, and the water will very often look distinctly light blue.

title: Bermuda - Hamilton Architecture (Plonkit)
description: Hamilton is by far the largest town on Bermuda, and as such, the downtown area is distinct due to its many large, densely built multi-floor buildings.

title: Bermuda - Grey Brick Buildings (Plonkit)
description: The northwestern tip of Bermuda can be recognised by the many large buildings made of unpainted grey brick.

title: Bermuda - Boat Trekker (Plonkit)
description: A boat trekker can be seen on the eastern coast of Bermuda. It can be seen going around Saint George’s Harbour and past Fort St. Catherine on the northeast tip of the island.

title: Canada - Maximum Speed (Plonkit)
description: Canada uses the word ‘maximum’ on speed signs. Because speed is measured in kilometres instead of miles, the numbers tend to be higher than the US which can be identifiable from afar.

title: Canada - Symbolic Signs (Plonkit)
description: Canadian road signs tend to be less wordy compared to their US counterparts. Good examples of this are railroad crossing and yield signs. In the US, these usually have the literal words ‘railroad crossing’ and ‘yield’ written on them, whereas in Canada, these signs are typically blank.

title: Canada - British English & Metric (Plonkit)
description: The English-speaking parts of Canada use British English spelling (e.g. centre; colour). In addition, Canada mostly uses the metric system. For example, speed is measured in kilometres per hour.

title: Canada - Canada Uses Unique (Plonkit)
description: Canada uses unique diamond-shaped T-Intersection signs.

title: Canada - Single Yellow Line (Plonkit)
description: Canadian roads usually have single yellow centre lines. However, double middle yellow centre lines are still decently common.

title: Canada - Gen 2 Halo (Plonkit)
description: Canada has a fair amount of Generation 2 coverage, especially in rural or remote areas. Generation 2 can be recognized by the big circular car blur and the halo-like colour distortion in the sky.

title: Canada - Gen 3 Mirrors (Plonkit)
description:
Generation 3 is significantly more common in Canada than in the US.
In addition, the side mirrors are blurred out differently: While they generally appear as two peaks in Canadian Gen 3 coverage, you will mostly see a single peak in the US.

title: Canada - Community Mailboxes (Plonkit)
description:
You can sometimes find communal mailboxes in Canada. Personal mailboxes are still very common, though.
Canada Post has a red logo, which sometimes appears on mailboxes.

title: Canada - Style Mailbox Resting (Plonkit)
description: This style of mailbox, resting on top of a post and with a small flag on the side, is mostly associated with North America.

title: Canada - Concrete Poles (Plonkit)
description:
North America primarily uses wooden utility poles.
Several European countries also primarily use wooden utility poles. However, a concrete pole in particular is mostly associated with Europe.
In addition, the US and Canada use transformers that are large metallic cylinders. This will never be seen in European countries.

title: Canada - Utility Poles (Plonkit)
description: This style of insulator, which is raised slightly on top of the utility pole, can be a good clue for the US and Canada. It is not typically found in Europe. It is especially apparent on simple poles with a single insulator.

title: Canada - License Plates (Plonkit)
description: The United States and Canada will usually have short license plates. Europe usually uses a long license plate which will also have a blue strip on the side.

title: Canada - Street Signs (Plonkit)
description: In the US and Canada, especially at large intersections, long metal bars with stop lights attached to them hang over the street. These bars also commonly have street signs, highway signs, or other signs attached to them.

title: Canada - Thin Metal Signposts (Plonkit)
description: Thin metal signposts are common. They will typically either have several small holes or have a U profile.

title: Canada - Water Towers Towns (Plonkit)
description: Water towers in towns across the United States and Canada are typically very tall, and sometimes have the name of the town on them.

title: Canada - Both Us And (Plonkit)
description: Both the US and Canada also have Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot. When the car isn’t blurred properly, you will usually see a mirror sticking out on the right side.

title: Canada - License Plates (Plonkit)
description:
Each province has its own unique licence plates, some recognizable from afar even when blurred. Multiple provinces do not require front plates, which can be useful when deciding between provinces.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Canada - French Language (Plonkit)
description: French is the majority language in Québec and parts of New Brunswick.

title: Canada - Highway Shields (Plonkit)
description:
Each province has their own highway shields with unique designs.
The green Trans-Canada Highway shield, shown in the top right of the image, can be found in all 10 provinces.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Canada - Kilometer Markers (Plonkit)
description:
Each province has its own unique kilometre markers that vary slightly.
Notably, Ontario KM markers have a white square at the bottom, which is unique to the province.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Canada - Province Speed Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Some provinces have unique speed signs.
Ontario speed limit signs may have a black section on the bottom with the words ‘km/h’ or ‘begins’ written in white.
British Columbian signs also include the ‘km/h’ but lack the black section.
Québec can sometimes have French on their speed limit signs.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.

title: Canada - Alberta Bollard (Plonkit)
description: Alberta has a unique black and white bollard that is often found at intersections. It has a cylindrical shape and two black bands that wrap all the way around. It is one of the most useful Canadian bollards to learn because it appears so frequently.

title: Canada - Manitoba Bollard (Plonkit)
description:
Manitoba uses black and grey painted bollards. Most of the time an orange stripe will be present below the grey one.
Wooden, rectangular bollards of this form are typically found further north in Manitoba.

title: Canada - BC Bollard (Plonkit)
description: British Columbia has black-and-white bollards with a thin, slightly curved shape. It is most commonly found on Vancouver Island, but can be found all throughout the province.

title: Canada - Quebec Guardrail Bollard (Plonkit)
description: Québec has unique bollards that are always attached to guardrails. They are long, thin white poles with a red or green reflector at the top.

title: Canada - Quebec Fire Hydrants (Plonkit)
description:
You will often find these yellow fire hydrant markers atop signposts in Québec.
In Québec City these markers will usually have a blue rectangle and markers in Trois-Rivières are distinctly small.

title: Canada - Quebec Road Markers (Plonkit)
description: You can find these rectangular markers on the sides of the roads in Québec. The colours can vary.

title: Canada - Ontario Road Markers (Plonkit)
description: You can find these diamond-shaped markers on the sides of the roads in Ontario. The colours can vary.

title: Canada - NWT Bollard (Plonkit)
description: The Northwest Territories has a black and white bollard with a cylindrical shape and two thick, black bands.

title: Canada - Transformer Orientation (Plonkit)
description: The transformers on poles will face the road in British Columbia and New Brunswick, while in other provinces, it will be parallel with the wires.

title: Canada - 45-Degree Transformers (Plonkit)
description: Transformers on Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia will be installed at a 45° angle relative to the road. On PEI, red numbers will usually be written on the side.

title: Canada - Qu Features (Plonkit)
description: Insulators facing towards or away from the road are mostly found in Québec, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island. Other provinces tend to have their insulators facing the same direction as the road.

title: Canada - Ontario Pole Tops (Plonkit)
description: These distinctive pole tops are most commonly found in Ontario. They have two insulators to the side, and one on top. The side insulators are affixed to the pole with a distinct attachment. Sometimes, multiple of them can be stacked on top of each other.

title: Canada - Quebec Angled Insulators (Plonkit)
description: Some Québec poles have recognizable pole tops with insulator rods that are angled slightly upwards.

title: Canada - Saskatchewan Alternating Insulators (Plonkit)
description: Pole top insulators in Saskatchewan alternate. While one pole will have one insulator on the left and two on the right, the next will have two on the left and one on the right.

title: Canada - Utility Poles (Plonkit)
description: Poles with two hanging insulators are common in Manitoba.

title: Canada - Quebec Pole Sticker (Plonkit)
description: Québec poles may sometimes have a vertical black and yellow label. There is a small ‘Q’ in the black part.

title: Canada - PEI Pole Sticker (Plonkit)
description: Poles on Prince Edward Island usually feature a small white sticker.

title: Canada - Quebec T-Signs (Plonkit)
description: Québec T-Intersection signs do not feature the chequerboard pattern.

title: Canada - Newfoundland T-Signs (Plonkit)
description: Newfoundland T-Intersection signs feature a rectangular yellow border around the diamond shape.

title: Canada - Green Backed Signs (Plonkit)
description: Road signs in British Columbia can have green backsides.

title: Canada - Hanging Signs (Plonkit)
description: Signs in British Columbia are sometimes hung down from these unique signposts.

title: Canada - Manitoba Sticker (Plonkit)
description: You can sometimes find a green and white striped sticker on signposts in Manitoba.

title: Canada - Saskatchewan Triangles (Plonkit)
description: Signposts in Saskatchewan can feature these white triangles. The number can vary.

title: Canada - Arrêt Signs (Plonkit)
description: Stop signs with the word ‘Arrêt’ are unique to Québec.

title: Canada - Bilingual Stop Signs (Plonkit)
description: Stop signs with both ‘Stop’ and ‘Arrêt’ are most commonly found in New Brunswick.

title: Canada - Street Signs (Plonkit)
description:
Like the stop signs, street signs in New Brunswick are also bilingual.
Though unlike the stop signs, bilingual street signs are found in other French minority areas of Canada.

title: Canada - Alberta Grid Roads (Plonkit)
description:
Rural roads in Alberta are numbered sequentially. This makes it easy to figure out your exact location using just a road sign.
- Township roads (Twp Rd) run east to west. Their numbers increase the more north you go.
- Range roads (Rge Rd) run north to south. Their numbers increase the more west you go. These numbers reset a couple of times.
This infographic shows which numbers are found where. You need to multiply the numbers on the grid by 10 to get the road numbers. For example, the junction in the image example is found just north of Red Deer.

title: Canada - Manitoba Grid Roads (Plonkit)
description:
Rural roads in Manitoba are organised in a grid and referred to only by their number and cardinal direction.
- Roads ending in N run east to west. Their numbers increase by one for every mile north of the US border.
- Roads with E or W run north to south. They tell you their position relative to the principal meridian, located just west of Winnipeg.
For instance, this image was taken 105 miles north of the US border and 147 miles west of the principal meridian.

title: Canada - Concrete Barriers (Plonkit)
description: British Columbia predominantly uses concrete barriers instead of guardrails.

title: Canada - Alberta Wire Guardrail (Plonkit)
description: This guardrail, with small poles connected by three or four metal wires, can rarely be found on major highways in Alberta.

title: Canada - Ontario Wire Guardrail (Plonkit)
description: In Ontario, you will often see these types of guardrails. They consist of cylindrical wooden posts, held together by precisely three metal wires. Some posts are marked by a reflective white band.

title: Canada - Newfoundland Pyramids (Plonkit)
description: In Newfoundland and Labrador, most wooden posts on guardrails have this pyramid shaped top. Occasionally, you can spot them on standalone posts and signposts as well.

title: Canada - Newfoundland Hydrants (Plonkit)
description: Fire hydrants in Newfoundland often have a diamond-shaped marker next to them.

title: Canada - Newfoundland Sign Boxes (Plonkit)
description: You can spot these wooden boxes holding up signs in Newfoundland and Labrador.

title: Canada - Within Eastern Canada (Plonkit)
description:
Within Eastern Canada, double yellow lines are most common in Nova Scotia, followed by Québec and Prince Edward Island. Ontario prefers single yellow lines for this purpose, but will occasionally use them.
For some empirical research, please see this document.

title: Canada - Dashed Middle Line (Plonkit)
description: You can sometimes find white dashes between the yellow centre lines in Saskatchewan.

title: Canada - Alberta Features (Plonkit)
description: Rumble strips in the centre of the road (generally over the roadlines) are most common in Alberta and British Columbia.

title: Canada - Ontario Traffic Cones (Plonkit)
description:
Ontario uses distinct orange and black striped traffic cones.
Québec, on the other hand, has unique orange and white striped traffic cones.

title: Canada - Quebec Chevrons (Plonkit)
description: Québec is the only Canadian province that uses red and white chevrons.

title: Canada - Rectangular Lampheads (Plonkit)
description: New Brunswick and Nova Scotia commonly use lampheads with a rectangular shape.

title: Canada - Curved Lamp Arms (Plonkit)
description: Lamp arms on utility poles in Nova Scotia are usually curved and much shorter than in the rest of Canada.

title: Canada - Newfoundland Wooden Bins (Plonkit)
description: Bins made of wood planks can be seen on Newfoundland driveways. These are most commonly octagonal, however they can have other shapes.

title: Canada - Western Mountains (Plonkit)
description: Western Canada is very mountainous. The highest mountains are in British Columbia, western Alberta, and parts of Yukon. Outside these provinces, large mountains are rare to non-existent in Canada.

title: Canada - Gen 2 Coverage (Plonkit)
description: Yukon has a very northern, boreal landscape that is mostly hilly, sometimes with large mountains in the distance. Coniferous trees line the roads and the further north you go, the thinner and shorter the trees get. Older Generation 2 coverage is common in this region.

title: Canada - BC Interior Landscape (Plonkit)
description: The landscape in the interior of southern British Columbia, mostly centred around the towns of Kamloops and Kelowna, has a distinct look. It is generally hilly and a little more arid than the rest of BC. The vegetation consists of sprawling brown grasslands, and pine tree forests on the hillsides.

title: Canada - Great Plains Landscape (Plonkit)
description: The Great Plains are mostly flat, with some rolling hills. There is a lot of agriculture, very few trees, and it is very sparsely populated. The landscape gets drier the further south-southwest you go, with the driest parts near the border with the US state of Montana.

title: Canada - Canola Fields (Plonkit)
description: Canola is grown in the central southern prairies, and it can be found almost nowhere else in Canada. It is visually similar to a field of bright yellow flowers.

title: Canada - Rouyn-Noranda Grid (Plonkit)
description: The region around Rouyn-Noranda in northwestern Québec can mainly be characterised by the north-south grid, along with the slightly hilly landscape featuring many agricultural fields nestled between the forests, which have many shorter trees as well as thin birches.

title: Canada - Saskatchewan Hills (Plonkit)
description: Southern Saskatchewan has many river valleys, which means that the province can have a barren hilly landscape; much more so than the rest of the Canadian Great Plains, which tends to be really flat.

title: Canada - Birch Forests (Plonkit)
description: Aspen trees are common in the forested parts of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. They are recognizable by their white, birch-like trunks. In most seasons, they have regular green leaves, but in fall coverage, they turn a characteristic bright yellow colour.

title: Canada - Canadian Shield (Plonkit)
description: The Canadian Shield extends through the eastern part of Canada. Therefore, you will commonly see exposed rocks on street view in the highlighted area.

title: Canada - Quebec-Windsor Corridor (Plonkit)
description: The Québec City-Windsor Corridor is the most densely populated part of Canada. It is mostly flat and green, with a patchwork of agriculture and occasional forest cover.

title: Canada - PEI Red Soil (Plonkit)
description: Prince Edward Island soil has a distinct red tint to it. Potato farming is also very common on PEI.

title: Canada - Balsam Fir (Plonkit)
description: The Balsam Fir is a very common species of tree found in Newfoundland. It has a Christmas tree-like appearance.

title: Canada - Area Code Map (Plonkit)
description:
Canadian phone numbers start with a three-digit area code. Both landlines and mobile phones use the same area codes.
You can click on the image to enlarge it.
